entries.title: Unfinished Business
entries.summary: Claire-Louise Bennett’s novels have found a new language to evoke the often circular, abstracted nature of human consciousness.
entries.source: The New York Review of Books
entries.content:
I once read that people who’ve had trauma to a particular part of the brain’s right hemisphere can develop a fixation on small, seemingly irrelevant objects. Walking into a room to do some task or other, they’ll get stuck obsessively staring at the door hinges. I don’t remember where I came across this fact—so much of what one reads these days slips into that great jumble of flotsam that drifts about the mind—but it occurred to me more than once while reading Claire-Louise Bennett’s books. Many passages begin in a straightforward way, with the setting of a scene and the promise of dramatic action. But then the story stalls, zeroes in on some incidental detail, and collapses into a mode of reflection that is circular and recursive. An early passage of her debut, Pond (2015), begins, “Sometimes a banana with coffee is nice.” The next four pages digress into aimless musings about a banana’s ideal state of ripeness, the best way to arrange almond flakes on a bowl of porridge, and the fact that oatcakes can also go nicely with coffee—so long as they’re the rough sort. This is before we’ve learned anything at all about the narrator whose consciousness will become the book’s subject and substance.

Bennett’s second book, Checkout 19 (2021), opens with an account, narrated in the collective “we,” of the experience of reading a book, a passage that begins as an encomium to the pleasures of literature but soon derails into a forensic analysis of the precise manner in which the eye travels across the words on the page:

When we open a book our eyes nearly always go over to the left page. That’s right—the left page, for reasons we have never previously reflected upon, has a much stronger pull on us than the right page. We always look down first of all at the right page. The right page first, that’s right. But the words on the right page always seem much too close. Too close to each other and too close to our face…. The words on the right seem far too eager, over-bearing, and yes somewhat ingratiating in fact, and very soon our rattled eyes leave the right page in order to seek refuge in the left.

The prose continues in this vein for several pages, considering how one must shift the book upward slightly after turning the page, and how it’s common to read the last sentences of the right side more hurriedly in anticipation of the turn. If Thomas Bernhard perfected, in his novels, the obsessive redundancy of human consciousness, Bennett captures this circularity at its most comically banal. The authorial voice that is supposed to be embarking on a story has gotten stuck, and the reader is stuck alongside her. We thought we were walking through a door, but instead our attention is continually returned to the construction of the door itself, reminded that we are reading a strange technology called a book.

That is, at any rate, what I take to be the purpose of the passage. As it happens, the first time I “read” Checkout 19, I was not reading at all. I’d downloaded the audiobook for a long drive across the Midwest, and as I left Chicago on the Dan Ryan Expressway, Bennett’s looping prose washed over me, invisibly and hypnotically, as I stared at a wide gray sky.

Bennett’s previous books, which sit somewhere in that generative no-man’s-land between novels and short story collections, are, to various degrees, invested in questions about literature, language, and reading. Pond, whose title is a nod to Thoreau’s Walden, details the quotidian life of an Englishwoman living alone in a cottage on the western coast of Ireland. The titular body of water has a sign next to it reading simply “Pond,” and the book was written, Bennett has said, during a period when she was “very fed up with semiotics and this notion that everything is a symbol or a sign.” It’s a problem that is not so easy to escape. The “Pond” marker is itself a sign in both senses of the word, emblematic, as the narrator puts it, of the “idiotic overlay of literal designations” that prevent us from moving about the world “in deep and direct accordance with things.” Checkout 19 is a coming-of-age story told through encounters with literature. It’s a book that captures the thrills of reading as a young person, when the written word is experienced as pure possibility, a state of prelapsarian innocence before language hardens into a collection of “literal designations” and familiar linguistic categories.

Bennett’s latest, Big Kiss, Bye-Bye, continues to explore these questions, this time through the problems of love, relationships, and desire. In the opening scene the narrator, a writer, arrives at a restaurant carrying a copy of her new book to give to her lover, Xavier, a much older man who was once a jet-setting private banker and is now living in a somewhat more modest style. He has periodically spent time in Mallorca, smoking weed and writing a memoir about his recollections of British high society in the 1960s and 1970s. Their relationship, which has been going on for nearly a decade, is romantic but minimally sexual, and has been fizzling out for some time, in part thanks to his age (he now uses a wheelchair and wears dentures). When he asks the narrator for a kiss, she refuses him. “I seem old to you?” he asks, to which she replies, “Yes…you are old, darling.” When she gives him her book, he comments on her author photo (“Cute little ears”). The reader is not privy to the subject of the book, or its genre, or its relationship to the narrator’s life, but a few days later Xavier emails her to say that he has read it and found it to be “some sort of HELL.” They do not speak again for several months.

During this mutual silence, the narrator leaves her apartment in the city and moves to the Irish countryside to live in a rented woodshed. For a long time she does not tell Xavier that she has left London and relishes the thought that he doesn’t know where she is. She goes on long hikes in the mountains and swims with friends in the sea. Most chapters are rendered in a diaristic present tense and begin with idle musings and trivial anxieties. The narrator recalls dreams she had the night before and worries about saved voicemails that have mysteriously disappeared. She documents the practical details of her life, which involve a lot of food and flowers and tend to evoke whatever the Irish version of hygge is: picking up port wine and cherries for a duck sauce. Drinking hot brandy after a swim in the sea. Risotto with mushrooms and hazelnuts. A gift of white lilies and red dinner candles.

Like a lot of prose that falls loosely under the heading of autofiction and that documents the life of a writer while they are doing everything except writing, the novel feels vaguely apophatic, as though we were seeing only the luminous rim of a light source that is otherwise obscured. We never learn more about the “HELL” that Xavier perceived in her book, nor anything at all about its contents. And while the narrator notes that “I haven’t written so much in eons,” there are no clues as to what she is working on.

This is, in fact, a recurring feature of the novel, which returns again and again to texts that are absent in one way or another: text messages and voicemails that remain unread or misplaced, letters that are lost in the mail. The narrator writes emails that she never sends, or composes them in her head without typing them out. One day while going through some old letters, she finds a copy of Xavier’s memoir (or what he calls his “bio”), which he asked her to read years ago, and which she never finished. (She told him that she’d lost it, embarrassed by some intimate details he’d included about their relationship.)

On another day she receives an email from her first publisher with a scanned letter from her A-level English teacher, who didn’t know how else to reach her. The teacher, Terence Stone, recently discovered that she’s become a writer, and he has some nice things to say about her books. The narrator replies, and they strike up an email correspondence, discussing Andrew Marvell and Wide Sargasso Sea, and reminiscing about other students and teachers, including a philosophy teacher named Robert Turner. “I had some dealings with him,” the narrator writes cryptically in one of her emails. “You probably know that.”

Later, she realizes that the letter forwarded to her by her first publisher was actually the copy of a letter Stone had written weeks earlier and sent to her second publisher. After realizing that this first letter might have been lost, he’d used a photo of the original to transcribe it word for word, and sent it to her first publisher. The narrator, who now possesses both letters (the first was eventually forwarded), reads them side by side—“I am well-practiced at comparing near identical versions of a text,” she notes—and finds that Stone had made a virtually perfect copy of the original, subtracting nothing and limiting his additions to two exclamation marks. “Imagine writing something out again and not being able to alter it,” the narrator marvels. “Not a single word!”

“A letter always arrives at its destination,” Lacan said in a 1955 lecture included in his Écrits. The aphorism occurs in his discussion of Edgar Allan Poe’s story “The Purloined Letter,” which revolves around a letter that is stolen and replaced with another without anyone reading it. For Lacan, the letter is a “pure signifier,” an object that is important not for its content but for its structural part in the story, which compels characters to repeat the same actions in scenes that mirror each other.

One senses that any given text in Big Kiss, Bye-Bye (and perhaps even the text of the novel itself) is more important structurally and formally than it is on its face. There’s something compulsive and dreamlike about the novel’s language, which is often deliberately redundant. Scenes and anecdotes recur across the novel—the memory of a former lover who spills coffee all over the bedcovers; her most recent encounter in a cemetery with Robert Turner, the philosophy teacher—but fail to become clearer through repetition. At times, the prose recalls not so much Bernhard or Gertrude Stein but a certain type of buggy LLM output known as repetition degeneration (sometimes called the “repeat curse”), in which the model gets stuck in self-reinforcing loops. (When asked to name as many books as possible, the LLM might answer “For example, Pride and Prejudice, written by Jane Austen, and The Great Gatsby for example, Pride and Prejudice, written by Jane Austen, and The Great Gatsby for example, Pride and Prejudice, written by Jane Austen, and the Great Gatsby…”) At one point the narrator asks herself why she’s sustaining the correspondence with Stone, projecting herself into the future: “And he will write back again. He will write back and I’ll write back and he’ll write back, and for how long will that go on for exactly, and why?”

The most prominent recurring loop in the narrator’s consciousness is her relationship with Xavier, which she spends a lot of time reflecting on during her early weeks in the countryside. Many of the conversations she recalls are so circular that they evoke domestic banter as pure form, more than any substantive communication. One chapter begins, without any establishing context:

“It’s as if several layers of skin have been removed,” I said. “That sounds like shingles,” he said. “That’s not how I meant it,” I said, “I was speaking metaphorically.” I don’t understand,” he said, “can’t you put it another way?” “Another way?” I said. “Yes,” he said, “I want to be able to understand.” “Well,” I said, that’s very considerate, but unnecessary—it won’t endure.” “Nevertheless,” he said. “Besides, it might come back.” “I’m sure it will,” I said.

Toward the end of this recalled scene, the narrator becomes fed up with Xavier’s questioning and confesses that she doesn’t want to describe what she’s feeling. “Some things are resistant to words maybe,” she tells him, “and when you start trying to apply them you end up with something else, another thing—a theory, I suppose.”

The narrator’s suspicious attitude toward language is most acute when she is confronted with the pressures of social decorum. While writing a letter to Stone, she realizes that it’s impossible to say anything direct or true because the whole tone of their correspondence is rooted in conventional pleasantries: “Polite, politus, polished. Smooth it all away, yes. Expunged. What the corps d’elite really care about is keeping things exactly as they are, because the way things are is jolly nice, thank you very much, it suits them very well.” She has the same beef with Christmas, a holiday that’s “ridiculous” because it is the same every year: “The same decorations, the same clothes, the same songs, the same food, the same sentiments…. It’s tedious and asinine yet everyone is trapped in it because nobody wants to let anyone else down.”

She eventually breaks the silence with Xavier, writing him a short email to say that she moved away a few months ago. She wants to remain friends with him and believes, even, that it is her “divine appointment” to be with him when he dies. But Xavier rebuffs her attempts to carry on a more platonic version of their relationship. “I will not exchange my LOVE for friendship,” he writes back. She starts to compose a reply, beginning with the sentence “It seems to me that you don’t know the first thing about love.” But then she stops, realizing that this is something she’s written to him countless times before. Love, in fact—and the effort to define or categorize it—was a recurring theme in their arguments over the years. She recalls some common refrains: “You have no idea what it means to love someone!” “Love asks nothing!” “I can’t believe we’re going through all this again!” But they do keep going through all that, again and again. Nowhere is the superfluousness of language so blatant as in a romantic relationship, where each quarrel echoes and recapitulates disagreements that have occurred in the past. In the end, she doesn’t finish the reply. “I deemed the email I had begun to write utterly pointless,” she reflects. “It said nothing new.”

In a 2016 interview with The Paris Review Bennett, whose novels capture the experience of consciousness more acutely than practically any other contemporary fiction, expressed skepticism about identifying too closely with her own mental activity. So much of what happens in the mind is repetitive, she said: “Habit creeps into thought and cuts off other more generative possibilities. Patterns, connections, associations, they occur quite naturally, don’t they?” If the recurrent scenes and images are occasionally frustrating, it’s because they reproduce, with a fidelity that is nearly intolerable, the well-worn circuits of the mind’s engine.

Writing can be a way out of this circularity: to put something down on paper is to transform the endless mental churn into a narrative that is linear and progressive. But Bennett is working within a strain of modernism that eschews order and clarity in favor of capturing the perpetually unfinished business of thinking, which is constantly undermining, undoing, and subverting its own conclusions. She has said that she agrees with Samuel Beckett’s assertion that the task of the artist is to “find a form that accommodates the mess,” an arguably self-defeating endeavor given that the very act of writing makes the fluidity of thought final and static. Once you put an experience into language, you end up with “another thing,” as the narrator of Big Kiss, Bye-Bye puts it.

The novel is, to a great extent, about this central paradox of language, its ability to simultaneously deepen and cheapen the immediacy of experience. The narrator recalls the magical power that certain words and phrases held for her as a young person. Even something as ordinary as the colloquialism “he has a chip on his shoulder” occasions, for the child who is encountering it for the first time, “little flares going off inside of you, briefly illuminating that dark innermost space, plethoric and phantasmal, that you don’t know very much about but sometimes feel yourself sinking into.”

When the novel eventually arrives at an extended memory of the narrator’s encounter in the cemetery with Robert Turner, the philosophy teacher she had “dealings with” as a young person and whom she calls her “first love,” the story takes an unexpected turn. The passage is narrated in the first-person plural (the voice that Bennett uses to depict the collective consciousness that exists before “female individuation,” as she puts it in Pond). At that point of our life, she notes of Turner, we did not know “what he was really like. Because obviously we were too young then to know what he was really like. Only now could we know. We were grown up now and knew how to know what people were like.”

The ability to put people into categories can be a protective measure, especially when the classification designates men with questionable intentions. But rather than presenting her “dealings” with Turner through the familiar lens of trauma and betrayal, the narrator expresses a longing to return to the mystery of unknowing, the madness of love, the curiosity about people that exists only when “we are at our most alert and sensitive and independent,” and when stories and love songs still possessed the capacity to deepen those feelings, giving them “dimension and tangibility and direction and new words.”

The scene reminded me of a passage in Pond, where the narrator recalls an erotic correspondence with a man. The hundreds of “lustful emails” they wrote to each other were so thrilling because the narrator had never before attempted that kind of writing. After deleting these messages, she wishes she’d kept them. “I won’t be able to write emails like that again you see,” she observes.

That’s to say I won’t be able to write emails like that for the first time again. And that really was what made them so exciting—using language in a way I’d not used it before, to transcribe such an intimate area of my being that I’d never before attempted to linguistically lay bare.

The relationship between the narrator of Big Kiss, Bye-Bye and Xavier similarly uses the erotic as a metaphor for the new and fleeting thrills of language, which inevitably lessen as we grow older, just as love ages and dims over time. Recalling her early days with Xavier, the narrator notes, “He said many other things during our apparently chaste rendezvous, impassioned admissions that I assumed I’d cherish forever, but in fact their poignancy soon faded.”

There are moments when the novel seems to be documenting the end of a love affair with language, a wistful and ambivalent good-bye to a medium that can no longer enchant in the way it once did. We live in a world that is entirely saturated with writing—with emails, text messages, the great ocean of language on the Internet, the inexhaustible machine-generated text that appears on the screen faster than the eye can consume it. The notion that we are moving into a postliterate era is not unrelated to this sense of overabundance. When the written word is cheap and widely available, it becomes harder than ever to see it as meaningful, like a currency that is devalued by inflation. Musing about the mystery of why she writes, the narrator of Big Kiss, Bye-Bye suddenly interjects: “Pfennig. Pfennig. Pfennig. They have gone now and the word has gone now. Can’t there be a new thing we call ‘pfennig’?” What would it mean to rename writing as “pfennig”? It’s a sly proposition, conveying the fear that language is a low-denomination coin that has fallen out of use—while also suggesting the possibility that it might be renewed.

In 2001 the electronic musician William Basinski found in his New York City loft a bunch of magnetic tapes that contained ambient “found” sounds he’d recorded in the 1980s. In the process of digitizing them, Basinski discovered that the tapes had been damaged. Rather than trying to restore them, he played them for extended periods, allowing them to deteriorate even more, which resulted in a series of short, haunting loops of sound, some with horns and strings, others featuring a metallic drone, like music heard through a thick wall or in a dream. The project, which was finished shortly before September 11 and which Basinski listened to as the Twin Towers collapsed, was released the next year as The Disintegration Loops.

Marshall McLuhan once argued that new media are “at first disguised as degradations of older media.” Each new technological medium is built on the content of the medium it has replaced. Film drew on the conventions of the novel and the theater. TV was built on the conventions of film. “The new form swallows, as it were, an older form,” he argues in his 1964 essay “New Media and the Arts,” an observation that holds up remarkably well six decades later. (The Internet has devoured TV; large language models have ingested the Internet.) McLuhan’s point was not just about technological mediums but about artistic forms as well. Hieronymus Bosch used the new rules of pictorial perspective as a container for medieval icons, just as Marlowe and Shakespeare used blank verse to swallow the medieval chronicle.

Big Kiss, Bye-Bye is less a novel than a technology that has swallowed the novel, a looping record of a genre that is disintegrating before our eyes. Its narrator speaks to us as a free-floating consciousness that has consumed countless scraps of books and letters, emails and lectures, and is trying to discover new wineskins for old wine. In the midst of her hypnotic prose, one occasionally hears echoes of other novels (“I would prefer to go into the shop and choose the flowers myself”) or literary remnants that have slipped off the page of one book and found themselves in another. When the narrator reads the passage in Huysman’s The Damned where Monsieur Durtal receives a letter from Madame Chantelouve written in “pale myrtle green ink,” she underlines it in a green ink of her own, “one of a slightly more robust hue.”

The narrator and Terence Stone have developed a habit of ending their emails to each other with literary allusions to greenness. It’s yet another novelty that has settled into the roteness of convention. At one point, eager to shake herself out of this pattern, the narrator observes, in a letter to him, that green is the color of death and decay as well as of new life:

Green is life is poison is sickness is peace is envy is fast is angelica is innocence is delirium is money is grass is chlorine is health is vomit is absinthe is tarnish is labyrinth is melancholy is nature is kryptonite is moss is gangrene is phantasmagoric is deceit is lush is infection is solitude is beginning is asparagus is putridness is secret is decay is spreading is tropical is nausea is mould is freshness is vitality is snot is lagoon is guilt is enchantment is mildew is vile is rampant is the colour of my ink yes, the colour of my ink, change, yes, instability, yes, life, life, yes, death, yes. Death. And the days, I write the days in green, and the things I need, the things I need—I write those in green too.

It’s possible to read this passage as a dead end: those who are a tad too literate, who have invested themselves too thoroughly in the notion that everything is a sign, eventually find that every object and idea, including the color of newness itself, cancels itself out with its opposite. The color comes to symbolize so much that it becomes meaningless. But there’s also something vigorous, nearly explosive, about this rush of language, as though it were a last-ditch effort to break through the impasse, driven by the enduring hope that writing might touch that totality of generative possibility that lies beyond language and can never fully be captured by it.

It’s easy to dismiss Bennett’s novels as language games that are formally clever but too conceptual to be enjoyed in any immediate, visceral sense. But after any extended immersion in her books, one feels bored with the plodding linearity of other novels, with their dutiful backstory and studied beats of narrative “reflection,” and is eager to return to that raw consciousness of Bennett’s narrators, who circle their subjects restlessly in the hope of stumbling on the unexpected. The signature tic of Bennett’s writing is a phrase, often following an observation, “Yes, that’s right.” It’s an expression that points backwards, to what was already said, but which has the effect of making the text feel spontaneously alive, as though the narrator were discovering what she is trying to say in the act of writing it, a perpetual becoming.

entries.title: The Sheer Size of It All
entries.summary: Edward Burtynsky’s photographs chronicle the gigantic scale of the scarred landscapes created by twentieth-century extractive industries.
entries.source: The New York Review of Books
entries.content:
Massive scale is a defining feature of the recent past. There were big things in antiquity—the pyramids of Egypt and Mexico; the Colossus of Rhodes, which stood at two thirds the height of the Statue of Liberty until an earthquake snapped it at the knees in 226 BCE—but there weren’t many of them. Not long ago I climbed to the top of St. Olaf’s Church in Tallinn, Estonia, which the tour guide claimed was the tallest building on earth into the seventeenth century; it was tall, but not what we’d call Tall. Not far from my home on the western shore of Lake Champlain lies the ore bed that in 1875 produced 10 percent of America’s iron ore; the #21 pit, once storied, stretches two hundred feet wide and three hundred feet deep. So—big. But a generation later, with the discovery of iron ore in Minnesota’s Mesabi Range, we begin to reach modern-scale Big. The Hull-Rust-Mahoning Mine in Hibbing (whose native son sang about it in “North Country Blues”) is three and a half miles wide, eight miles long, and 535 feet deep. There’s a visitor’s center on the edge offering a view, though it had to be moved in 2019 to allow for the expansion of the mine.

The Canadian photographer Edward Burtynsky is perhaps the greatest chronicler of that era of scale, which stretched across the long twentieth century and only now shows the first signs of receding. He managed, by accident of geography and timing and by dint of temperament and technological skill, to be perfectly placed to make this new gigantism legible. The son of Ukrainian immigrants, he grew up in St. Catharines, Ontario, where his father worked at a General Motors plant. Early in his new biography of Burtynsky, James King quotes him describing a youthful visit to the factory:

At the age of seven I saw engines being cast and steering knuckles being stamped out of red-hot ingots held with tongs by men in silver suits on massive forge presses that shook the ground and could be heard halfway across the city.

He could ride his bike to the Welland Canal, which routed maritime traffic around Niagara Falls between Lake Ontario and Lake Erie. He traded fruit with the sailors for cigarettes: “I remember being overwhelmed by the scale of the ships.” After working for a while at the GM plant (removing carcinogenic PCBs from machines on the assembly line), he moved to Toronto in his mid-twenties to study photography at the Ryerson Institute of Technology:

I remember the first time I came to Toronto alone. I found myself looking up at skyscrapers… I was bowled over by the scale at which we operate, the kind of things we can create. For things to be on this scale, I thought, there has to be something equally monumental in the landscape where we have taken all this material from.

That insight accounted for his first great works. After early studies of taxidermy and local farming, he found his eye in the early 1980s with a series of images of mines and quarries, subjects he has returned to again and again. These are the negative spaces that supplied the material for the spectacular constructions of our modern world. Some of his first successful images came from the Rock of Ages quarry in Barre, Vermont, at six hundred feet the world’s largest deep-hole granite quarry:

I would find the right location and then light up a hash spliff just enough to shift my perception and dial down the noise in my head yet not altering enough that I would be unsafe standing on edges of the quarries on broken and unstable rocks.

The images he produced were serene and geological, a record of deep time as much as of space, and they were popular—he made enough to bail out his flailing Toronto darkroom. Soon he was headed for the marble quarries of Carrara in Italy, sometimes with his lens focused on the rock and sometimes backing up far enough to situate the quarries in the surrounding mountains and forests.

He broadened his work to other mines: his home province of Ontario provided the cautionary tale of Sudbury, where nickel mining and smelting and its associated pollution had produced a dead zone of astonishing proportion, and Elliot Lake, once among the largest uranium mines on earth, whose tailings had overflowed the surrounding landscape, wiping out much of the surrounding forest. He moved on to other kinds of “mines”—the graveyards where discarded metal was condensed into cubes, the great piles of tires that stretched for many acres across the California landscape. One of those piles (in an abandoned quarry) had caught fire two years before and was still burning:

Intrigued by the image this evoked, we set out with all my equipment to go and take a look. It was an apocalyptic scene, and we could only stay for about twenty minutes because of the splitting headaches and wheezing lungs brought on by the smoke and tire fumes.

Burtynsky’s work is not particularly judgmental—there’s beauty to be found even in these objectively ugly scenes. But his task seems to be recording the sheer size of it all, an effort simply to chronicle what mankind at this moment was doing.

There’s a useful contrast to be made with the other great photographer mining this vein (sometimes literally), Burtynsky’s friend Sebastião Salgado. It is as if, unconsciously and as a matter of temperament, they had divided up the work, with Salgado’s much more politically charged photos concentrating on the workers involved in extraction while Burtynsky viewed the resulting landscapes. The division is by no means absolute, and Burtynsky has many fine shots of people involved in these projects, but the differences are telling. Salgado, for instance, produced a memorable series of images in the 1990s of “ship-breakers” on the beaches of Bangladesh—companies disposing of giant seagoing vessels would run them aground at high tide, and armies of men would descend to take them apart for scrap, a dangerous form of mining that completed the industrial cycle. Salgado wrote, “I wanted to pay homage to all the men and women who built the world around us,” and his pictures capture the brutality of the work.

Burtynsky followed him to the Bay of Bengal a few years later, photographing similar scenes on the Indian coast, but his eye focused on “a landscape littered with rusting colossi that loomed silently over scores of workers.” He said later:

One can look at these images as making political statements about the environment, but they also celebrate the achievements of engineering or the wonders of geology…. I’m not using my art to browbeat corporations for the rack and ruin of our landscape. I’m trying [to cut] a slice out of the chaos and give [it] visual coherence so that the viewer can decide.

In any event, King writes, the two weeks of shooting on the beach in 2000 produced twenty-four images that “emphasize the size of the vessels, as huge, hideous sculptures that exist in a sinister twilight.” He’s right, I think, to pair them in his book with an image of Richard Serra’s giant sheets of rusting steel at the Guggenheim Museum Bilbao. Monumentality really is part of Burtynsky’s brief. He became expert at photographing from helicopters and then from drones, and his show at the International Center of Photography last summer included a thirty-by-thirty-foot image of a High Plains Texas industrial farmscape taken from thousands of feet up; it was, if you think about it, a picture of a mine extracting fertility from the soil (and water from the depleting aquifers beneath it) to produce cheap plenty.

In his effort to understand our time on earth, Burtynsky had to figure out how to chronicle its single most important element. Oil unleashed the mobility that rewrote the American landscape and produced both the highest concentrations of wealth and its greatest and most democratic spread; it powered the militaries of the twentieth century and also gave them something to fight over. But it’s not the easiest thing to take a picture of: the “mining” happens deep underground, where a drill bit punctures a reservoir, and the resulting product is (hopefully) contained inside a series of pipes and tanks up to the moment when it leaves your tailpipe in a (largely invisible) cloud of carbon dioxide and various trace gases. Burtynsky took some haunting images of fields full of oil derricks, both in California and in Baku, Azerbaijan, the site of the world’s first big offshore oil fields. He also photographed in the tar sands of Alberta, perhaps the single biggest scar humans have inflicted on the planet. But I think his more important achievement was to figure out how to depict the consumption of oil.

Three pictures in particular—all of which were in the ICP show—seem crucial to me. The first is a sweeping shot of the NASCAR races at Alabama’s Talladega track, where spectators have gathered to watch (and perhaps more importantly to listen to) this festival of internal combustion. “Such races have been photographed many times,” he said, “but I am interested in tying it in with the body of work I have done as an expression of the scale of motor culture, where everybody is rallying around the machine.” No image has captured American automotive joy with such clarity.

The second and third images are more mixed. One is of a crowded stretch of highway-adjacent roadway in Breezewood, Pennsylvania, filled with the neon logos of our age—Exxon, Shell, and Sunoco dominate, but so do McDonald’s and Subway and Starbucks; to the standard American eye it manages to be both cluttered and relaxing. The other, which David Campany uses as the cover of the catalog for the ICP show, is of Scottsdale, Arizona. It’s perfectly bifurcated by a road: on one side, an Indian reservation, it’s essentially untouched desert; on the other it’s a suburb crowded with tiled roofs, swimming pools, and enormous suburban houses. If it weren’t so absorbing, it would be a touch didactic.

Still, the most important result of this era was essentially invisible: the concentration of colorless CO2 building up in the atmosphere as the coal and gas and oil combusted. The greenhouse effect came to public notice just as Burtynsky’s career was taking off, with James Hansen’s 1988 congressional testimony roughly coinciding with his first important images. But the irony of global warming was that it was, for several decades, largely impossible to see. I can remember photographers phoning me in those early years to ask what they should be taking pictures of. Only a few managed to really pull it off, perhaps most notably James Balog, who used time-lapse photos to great effect in his Chasing Ice series, which documented the decline of the great glaciers.

In recent years it’s become tragically easy to document the floods and fires that climate change is now producing (though the biggest effects, on systems like the jet stream and the Gulf Stream, remain hard to render). Burtynsky supplied one of the most important of these images last year, just in time to make the ICP show, where it was hung at the last minute next to the cash register but too late to be included in the catalog. It’s an aerial shot of the aftermath of the fire at Pacific Palisades in Los Angeles in January 2025, with insanely crisp detail of the ashy remains of one house after another. It shows the ultimate end of all that oil, in a kind of mirror image of the suburban sprawl he’d captured in Arizona and elsewhere. It was the most gripping picture on view.

Burtynsky is at the height of his powers, and far be it from me to suggest where he should train his lens. But I’m taken by the idea that he may be well suited to document the next, perhaps more hopeful, era in our large-scale interaction with our environment. Burtynsky shot many great series of China’s rise as a manufacturing power—enormous photos of enormous factories, with uncountable ranks of workers producing the endless collection of inexpensive stuff that marks the early twenty-first century. But now many of those factories are turning out solar panels and wind turbines, which are being installed in China and around the world at a remarkable pace.

In one sense this is just a continuation of the old story—and Burtynsky has produced a haunting image (in some ways, I think, a paean to the late Salgado) of an African mine supplying the cobalt necessary for some of these remarkable machines. But in another sense these are quite different products. Instead of extracting fossil fuels, they harvest the inexhaustible resources of sun and wind; the mining required is to build the machines, not to fuel them. Over time, if they spread, our impact on the earth should begin to recede, or at least to change—nearly half the shipping on the planet, for instance, carries hydrocarbons back and forth across the seas to be burned, an increasingly unnecessary task. Fields of solar panels take up space, but much more benignly than what they replace; farmers are discovering that the shaded rows they create are excellent for growing many crops.

Industrial postmodernity needs a chronicler, and it would be poetic if Burtynsky were able to end his career documenting at least the start of the massive repair project that one hopes will come to occupy our species.

entries.source: The New York Review of Books
entries.content:
No, no, I don’t believe in my poems,

Not really, but I defer to the poet in me

Who belies belief with a fact that

Requires no belief, to write a poem

In which fire is the poetic

Element, fire burning in a wood

At night, the leaves falling in flames

From trees, and he lets this poem mean

All that poetry infers but does not say

Because, to him, a poem doesn’t say

All that it means but keeps the silent

Stillness of a wood after the fire dies,

And smoke rising from the ash.

entries.title: Work Poem
entries.summary: I’m too broke to make the work Or I don’t care enough about the work To be as broke as I should let myself be To have the time to make the work I work too hard to make the work Or my indolence is too great to take that pleasure In the work that […]
entries.source: The New York Review of Books
entries.content:
I’m too broke to make the work

Or I don’t care enough about the work

To be as broke as I should let myself be

To have the time to make the work

I work too hard to make the work

Or my indolence is too great to take that pleasure

In the work that the work needs

Or once I arrive as a boat from sea

At the limits of my intelligence

I quail and put the work away

I do not push the work or

Push the work too hard

So the work becomes working

A tough dough, not play

That I want to have fun, to see

The delights of the world

With my eyes and drink wine and say

This is the work of the work

Let it relinquish me, tame

Monster, to roam freely among the delights of the world

That yet I travel too lightly, quaffing

The brine of forgetfulness, that I should stay

In some hermitage and let the work of the world

Be, for it circles fine

Without me, that the medium

Of the work is inauthentic and circumscribes

The world of works in false conceit,

Belt that begets its own limitations, that

I speak these words I call my ideas

But lack their commitments

That, gadfly I, delight to say

I am working on

I am working on, and the work

A boat tossed at sea

Never arrives.

No, these are not paradisiacal thoughts.

They do not befit

This situation, which is that of the garnet

In the anguish, the anguish

In the garnet, the cities

In the anguish, in the garnet

All correspondence, all array

And its open, raw, unlikely vitality.

entries.content:
Because the islands bright white          solid stone

Reach down through shifting mud beneath the creek

Except what might be seen          by radar meek

Orisons sounding the meek’s due          but none

Near for use          things lost in their pocks are gone

Never to be regained          I lost a week

Ago an action          figure’s golden beak-

Shaped mask in the dark          and I’ve come back alone

Today again to search the plunging edge

As I have come each day          and stood unwilling

Yesterday and before afraid and stand

Looking at the dark water          who will dredge

Open the bed          and risk the vipers and

Refresh the toy with which I practice killing

entries.title: The Plot to Delete Democracy
entries.summary: In The Nerd Reich Gil Durán shows how Silicon Valley billionaires have pushed a fringe ideology—what is popularly called techno-fascism but is closer in aspiration to straight-up totalitarianism—into the affairs of state.
entries.source: The New York Review of Books
entries.content:
Chances are you already know some random things about the Silicon Valley technology billionaires who have embraced—and been embraced by—the Trump administration: that, for example, Peter Thiel’s data mining company, Palantir, supplies surveillance software to Immigration and Customs Enforcement, that the recent public stock offering for SpaceX briefly made Elon Musk the world’s first trillionaire, or that the venture capitalist Marc Andreessen, a former Democratic Party stalwart, turned to Trump after he saw, he said, the most successful people sending “their kids to the most politically radical institutions, which teach them how to be America-hating communists.” You may even know that Thiel, in contrast to most of his Silicon Valley peers, supported Trump’s 2016 campaign, or that during the 2024 campaign Musk was Trump’s largest individual donor, giving $239 million to his pro-Trump America PAC and around $50 million to other Trump-aligned groups, or that Andreessen helped staff the Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE), Musk’s predatory duchy within Trump’s second administration.

Yet in the fractured attention economy in which we all now reside, it’s easy to know these disparate facts and still have only a vague understanding of their larger significance. It is the mastery of such diverse particulars that makes Gil Durán’s new book, The Nerd Reich: Silicon Valley Fascism and the War on Democracy, so valuable. Durán, the former editorial page editor of the San Francisco Examiner, has taken a tremendous amount of previously reported information that, on its own, might have looked like dots on a pointillist’s canvas, and created a haunting picture of the political project pursued and abetted by a confederacy of Silicon Valley elites. Their goal is nothing less than to destroy liberal democracy. Their money, in tandem with a Republican Party establishment that shares many of their objectives and a president with an insatiable lust for riches, has pushed a fringe ideology—what is popularly called technofascism but is closer in aspiration to straight-up totalitarianism—into the affairs of state.

Democracy has always been vulnerable to capture by those who would use its own apparatus to undermine it. While the United States has long harbored people and parties that have espoused antidemocratic sentiments—the Know-Nothing and Communist parties come to mind—the Supreme Court’s 2010 ruling in Citizens United v. Federal Election Commission presented an unprecedented opportunity for those willing to spend whatever it takes to elect politicians to do their bidding. According to a report by the Roosevelt Institute,

The 2024 federal elections saw the highest level of billionaire spending in American history. In an effort to influence outcomes, billionaire donors and their families spent over $2.6 billion—a figure amounting to nearly 20 percent of total federal election spending that cycle.

Most of this money went to support Donald Trump’s reelection. Trump’s 2025 One Big Beautiful Bill Act then rewarded his billionaire friends (as well as his own family) with enormous tax cuts. But Trump’s Silicon Valley backers, who together donated nearly $400 million to his campaign, wanted something more: for the newly reelected president to demolish the federal bureaucracy and its pesky regulatory regime.

Decimating the so-called administrative state has long been advocated by right-wing partisans. In his 1981 inaugural address, for example, Ronald Reagan vowed to “curb the size and influence of the Federal establishment,” and the following year he convened the Grace Commission to root out “government waste.” (It did not, as Congress failed to implement most of its recommendations.) Twelve years later the Republican campaign platform Contract with America promised to “transform the way Congress works,” which “would be the end of government that is too big, too intrusive, and too easy with the public’s money.” Though Republicans were able to win a majority in the House—their first in forty years—their ambitions were largely stymied by a resistant Senate and the veto power of the Democratic president, Bill Clinton.

In 2024 Musk, fresh from pulverizing Twitter and imbued with the “move fast and break things” ethos of Silicon Valley, was not interested in such niceties as advisory boards or legislation. As he ingratiated himself with Trump by becoming his biggest donor, Musk pitched him on creating a strike force aimed at eliminating what he believed to be the excesses of the federal government. In keeping with the quid pro quo that has come to define Trump’s presidency, Trump issued Executive Order 14158, “Establishing and Implementing the President’s ‘Department of Government Efficiency,’” on his first day in office. And he put Musk in charge, along with the tech billionaire Vivek Ramaswamy (who soon departed and is now running for governor of Ohio).

DOGE was a first run of what Durán calls “the nerd reich”: two incredibly rich guys who worship at the altar of money and technology taking an ax to federal agencies they didn’t like, such as USAID (which Musk called “a criminal organization”), slashing the budgets of the National Institutes of Health (too woke) and the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (whose functions, Project 2025 claimed, could be privatized and monetized), firing tens of thousands of workers, and causing hundreds of thousands of others to take buyouts or early retirement. It was disruptive, cataclysmic, and cruel—so in that sense it was a roaring success. Financially, on the other hand, it was an abject failure. Though Musk promised that DOGE would cut $2 trillion from the federal budget, not only did it not come anywhere close to that figure, its “savings claims [were] overstated, inaccurate and rooted in a fundamental misunderstanding of how the federal budget works,” according to a report by NPR, further substantiated by a recent Government Accountability Office investigation. Musk stepped down after 130 days.

Advertisement

Musk’s departure was not the end of DOGE. Russell Vought, one of the main architects of Project 2025, the Heritage Foundation’s blueprint for restructuring the government, whom Trump installed as director of the Office of Management and Budget, took over. A canny right-wing operative and avowed Christian nationalist who harbors a persistent disaffection for democracy, Vought was in a position to set DOGE (through the OMB) on a course to implement his vision of an autocratic, post-constitutional government. In a private speech in 2023, he said:

We want the bureaucrats to be traumatically affected. When they wake up in the morning, we want them to not want to go to work because they are increasingly viewed as the villains. We want their funding to be shut down so that the EPA can’t do all of the rules against our energy industry because they have no bandwidth financially to do so.

Vought championed what Trump called the Merit Hiring Plan, which required applicants for government vacancies to write short essays professing their patriotism and fealty to the president and his policies; seeded slash-and-burn emissaries throughout the government; and strong-armed Congress into accepting a $9.4 billion rescissions package that eliminated funding for programs maligned by the right, such as the Corporation for Public Broadcasting and the US Institute of Peace. According to a study by The American Prospect, drawing on a study by the Revolving Door Project, “DOGE was—and remains, through Vought’s OMB—an effort to extinguish the existing government and create a new one in the image of oligarchs and far-right ideologues.”

It would be inaccurate, though, to suggest that Musk’s departure from DOGE and Vought’s ascendancy represent the supremacy of the inveterate right-wing establishment over the upstart tech billionaires. Not only are the two in many ways ideologically aligned; Vought’s think tank, the Center for Renewing America, operates within a conservative ecosphere that benefits from dark money groups such as DonorsTrust and the Rockbridge Network, a “political venture capital firm” cofounded by J.D. Vance. Both DonorsTrust and Rockbridge are bankrolled in large part by Silicon Valley’s most prominent Trump supporter, the man who once famously wrote, “I no longer believe freedom and democracy are compatible”: Peter Thiel.

As Durán points out, Thiel’s politics precede Trump—indeed, they precede his own engagement with electoral politics by decades. As a Stanford undergraduate in the late 1980s he cofounded The Stanford Review as a counterweight to what he later said was the “wokeness” of the university (though the pejorative shorthand for progressive views hadn’t yet entered the right-wing lexicon). The Stanford Review attracted a group of like-minded students, many of whom later joined Thiel’s tech ventures and became very rich and aggressively doctrinal themselves.

David Sacks, for example, the editor-in-chief of The Stanford Review a few years after Thiel and the coauthor with him of the 1995 book The Diversity Myth: Multiculturalism and Political Intolerance on Campus (in which they argued, among other things, that the definition of rape had been expanded to include “seductions that are later regretted”), became an executive at Confinity, the precursor to PayPal, of which Thiel was a cofounder. When PayPal sold to eBay for $1.5 billion in 2002, he became an extremely wealthy man. Sacks is now the cochair of Trump’s Council of Advisors on Science and Technology, after a turn as the administration’s special adviser for AI and crypto; in that position he, among other things, worked to preempt state AI regulations. Crucially, as The New York Times reported, Sacks’s dual roles as the administration’s AI and crypto “czar,” influencing policy for both technologies while also investing in them, “laid the groundwork for his investments to flourish.”

Trump, who once called Bitcoin “a scam,” embraced cryptocurrency in his second term, creating his own crypto company with the members of his family; according to Durán, “Within a few months of his return to the White House, the Trump family’s net worth increased by $5 billion.” A recent New York Times investigation found that another crypto scheme, a Trump meme coin, netted the president hundreds of millions of dollars, while his wife took in $6 million from her cryptocurrency. In contrast, the Times noted that many of the small investors who bought these coins lost their money.

Advertisement

Beyond Trump’s self-dealing, his sudden affection for cryptocurrency has created an undetectable way for foreign nationals to ingratiate themselves with him, raising national security concerns. Consider Guren “Bobby” Zhou, a former flooring salesman and failed investor from China who had come under investigation for money laundering in the UK. Zhou put $100 million into Trump’s World Liberty Financial cryptocurrency. As the Times noted:

In any prior era, a windfall for the president of that size from a foreigner with no public signs of access to that level of wealth would have certainly gone against norms and might have spawned a congressional investigation.

Instead, the curious case of Mr. Zhou illustrates the ease with which buyers with unknown backgrounds and motivations can use the anonymity of cryptocurrency to shower Mr. Trump with money.

It remains unclear who fronted Zhou the money.

Though it may not have been obvious to the public when Thiel and his partners started Confinity, their mobile payments app PayPal was also aimed at bypassing the traditional banking system. (Confinity later merged with Musk’s digital payment platform, X.com, and took the name PayPal.) As Max Chafkin points out in his book about Thiel, The Contrarian (2021):*

From its earliest days Thiel understood that it could be a lot more than a clever way to split checks…. If it took off, it would make it impossible for governments to regulate their economies, leading to, he boasted to a reporter, “the erosion of the nation-state.”

It was the first volley in an attack on state control that almost no one buying stuff on eBay knew they were engaged in.

Durán traces Thiel’s antiestablishment heterodoxy to a 1997 book called The Sovereign Individual, written by James Dale Davidson, an American venture capitalist and the founder of the conservative National Taxpayers Union, and William Rees-Mogg, a former editor of The Times of London and a life peer in the House of Lords. The book, Durán writes,

laid out a dramatic thesis, hyping the arrival of an information age in which technology would upend both economics and politics, eliminating most jobs, reducing work to piecemeal gig assignments, and sparking widespread decline, chaos, and violence as tens of millions of people struggled to survive without work.

He continues:

Davidson and Rees-Mogg argued that technological disruption would accelerate the sorting of humanity into inferior and superior people. Their cognitive elites would be investors and tech entrepreneurs with the skills and knowledge to prosper in the new decentralized tech economy. They would become a powerful new political force, a class of “sovereign individuals” whose intelligence and wealth freed them from democracy, nationality, taxes, and regulations. “Cybercurrency”—an early term for crypto—would aid their escape and fuel their rise.

Certainly, as prescient as this seems now, it’s also possible to see the book as a formula followed by those “cognitive elites” to create the conditions to promote their domination. Bitcoin, the first mainstream cybercurrency, wasn’t “mined” until 2009, twelve years after The Sovereign Individual was published. Thiel’s Founders Fund was one of the earliest venture firms, along with Andreessen Horowitz, to invest heavily in it, thus offering Bitcoin legitimacy, which encouraged public and institutional adoption, which then increased its “value.” Both companies also hold significant amounts of Ether, the native cryptocurrency of the blockchain network Ethereum, Bitcoin’s nearest competitor. Ethereum was invented by the Russian Canadian programmer Vitalik Buterin while he was supported by the Thiel Fellowship, which rewarded young people—Buterin was twenty—with $100,000 to drop out of university or forgo it altogether to build new technologies.

Meanwhile, the gig economy Davidson and Rees-Mogg imagined came to fruition with the introduction of such platforms as Uber (2009) and Airbnb (2008), which received investments from Sacks (Uber) and Thiel (Airbnb), who were not averse to making scads of money while disempowering workers. Even the newsletter platform Substack, which established a gig economy for journalists (including Durán) just as the newspaper business was shrinking, traces its creation to the tech incubator Y Combinator, which was run by Sam Altman, the guy who keeps warning that the product being developed by his current company, OpenAI, is an existential threat to humanity or at least to workers everywhere. (Altman, who was a six-figure donor to Joe Biden’s 2020 presidential campaign but on July 4, 2025, declared himself “politically homeless,” donated $1 million to Trump’s inauguration fund and $5 million to his super PAC, MAGA Inc.) Thiel was a partner at Y Combinator at the time, and Andreessen Horowitz was one of Substack’s initial major investors. While Substack newsletters enable writers to monetize their work, they also shrink the public square—which, in Durán’s estimation, is the actual point.

Here’s Balaji Srinivasan, a former partner at Andreessen Horowitz and the author of The Network State: How to Start a New Country (2022): “We replace media with parallel media…. They’re gaining strength. They’re pulling away users—until they become the new thing. So this is how we turn that seemingly impossible thing of building a new country.” A network state, as Srinivasan defines it, is “a highly aligned online community with a capacity for collective action that crowdfunds territory around the world and eventually gains diplomatic recognition from pre-existing states.” Or as he said on a podcast called Moment of Zen, “What I’m really calling for is something like tech Zionism.”

A more functional definition is offered by the St. Lawrence University professor Zane Griffin Talley Cooper: “The Network State model seeks to eschew most forms of social and environmental regulation, instead promoting a libertarian fantasy of rapid privatized innovation and development.” That fantasy is becoming something of a reality, thanks in part to Pronomos Capital, a venture firm run by Patri Friedman, the grandson of Milton Friedman, that supports a worldwide collection of what its website calls, with ardent vagueness, “the cities of tomorrow.” Srinivasan is an adviser to Pronomos; Thiel is an investor. (Friedman has also promoted building autonomous, extrajudicial cities floating on the ocean.)

Not long after the publication of his book, Srinivasan convened a conference in Amsterdam that highlighted network state projects already underway in San Francisco, Arizona, Texas, Honduras, and Zanzibar. There have been other conferences since; the 2025 Network State Conference attracted over eight thousand participants and featured such speakers as Buterin, Ben Horowitz, and Bryan Johnson of “Don’t Die” fame. Durán writes that a Pronomos-backed project called Praxis, led by a twenty-eight-year-old named Dryden Brown, “announced plans to build a tech city in the Mediterranean backed by Sam Altman, Joe Lonsdale, and Srinivasan himself, along with investments from Thiel and others.” (Lonsdale, another Stanford Review and PayPal alum, is a cofounder of Palantir.) It’s not clear exactly how California Forever, a real estate venture funded by a group of tech billionaires who secretly bought around 60,000 acres of land sixty miles north of San Francisco in order to build a new, improved city, fits into Srinivasan’s vision, but Durán reports that on the Moment of Zen podcast, Srinivasan “added that a major new network state project was already underway ‘on bare land’ in California,” a claim its CEO, Jan Sramek, a former Goldman Sachs trader, has denied.

Most recently, Durán reports, proponents of what are also known as “freedom cities” have been eyeing Greenland as an outpost for an unregulated tech haven where artificial intelligence and bio-hacking experiments could be developed without guardrails or government interference. In response to Trump’s interest in claiming the Danish autonomous territory for the United States, Brown tweeted:

Praxis would like to support Greenland’s development by coordinating talent, companies, and capital to help secure the Arctic, extract critical resources, terraform the land with advanced technology to make it more habitable, and build a mythical city in the North.

The previous summer Brown had gone to Greenland “to try to buy it,” but was rebuffed, as was Trump’s emissary, Vance. (Vance, of course, is yet another Thiel protégé, and Thiel’s $15 million donation to Vance’s 2022 Senate campaign was the largest ever given to a Senate candidate. Two years later Thiel lobbied Trump to choose Vance as his running mate.) Still, despite Greenlanders’ hostility to these overtures, the Greenland saga is not over. Brown told Reuters that even after his ill-fated trip other groups had expressed their interest in establishing a new domain in Greenland, and Trump himself has not given up on his territorial ambitions, as he made clear to the Danes and other erstwhile allies at a NATO summit in early July. In August an oil company linked to Trump began setting up drilling infrastructure on the island’s east coast without permission from Greenlandic authorities.

Srinivasan’s notion of parallel institutions also extends to money and banking, education (replace Harvard with the Thiel Fellowship), and the government itself. In June 2022, shortly before the publication of The Network State, a group of tech billionaires and venture capitalists led by Garry Tan, one of the original Palantir employees, who later became the head of Y Combinator, pursued a multimillion-dollar campaign that ousted San Francisco’s progressive district attorney, Chesa Boudin, and three members of the school board. It was a bald demonstration of the power of tech money to bend politics to its will. For Srinivasan, though, it was not enough. “It may be easier to start a new city than to reform San Francisco,” he tweeted to his one million followers, during the recall campaign. On the Moment of Zen podcast, Durán writes, Srinivasan was more explicit: “The goal, he said, was to do to San Francisco what Musk had done to Twitter: Gut it, purge it, and harvest its power.”

More than Srinivasan, the most influential proponent of gutting and purging is the lachrymose, self-appointed philosopher king Curtis Yarvin, who, writing online as Mencius Moldbug, dispensed his nihilistic, burn-it-all-down militancy on a blog called Unqualified Reservations. “The other day I was tinkering around in my garage and I decided to build a new ideology,” he wrote in his first post in 2007. That ideology, which owes a debt to Ayn Rand, Carl Schmitt, Murray Rothbard, and a mash of other libertarian, fascist, and authoritarian janissaries, portrays democracy as a failed system that needs to be replaced by a national CEO, also known as, he wrote, “a dictator.” Durán points to an early essay of Yarvin’s in which he imagines a San Francisco governed by “a totalitarian corporation called Friscorp. This corporate overlord would keep its residents under constant surveillance and exercise total power over their lives. Friscorp could even execute its residents without cause.” (After the unprovoked shooting deaths of Renee Good, Alex Pretti, and Johan Guerrero by federal agents without consequences so far, this scenario feels less theoretical.) Anticipating Srinivasan’s network state concept, Yarvin also argued that people should array themselves in small city-states governed by joint-stock corporations where they would have no rights. If they were unhappy, they could vote with their feet by relocating to a different corporate entity.

As outlandish as Yarvin may seem, it would be foolish to dismiss him. Yarvin is widely credited as being the resident philosopher of what’s known as the “Thielverse,” which includes Vance, Srinivasan, Buterin, and Andreessen, among many others. (In 2013 Thiel and Andreessen Horowitz funneled more than $1 million into a company Yarvin was starting.) And as Thiel and his associates have insinuated themselves into Trump’s world, they have brought Yarvin’s ideas with them. “With the help of men like Thiel,” Durán writes, “Yarvin’s radically unhinged ideas evolved from a blogger’s musings into a serious effort to undo democracy that would be adopted by a presidential administration.”

Two days before Trump’s second inauguration, at a party at Thiel’s D.C. redoubt, the incoming vice-president, Vance, greeted Yarvin with the hail-fellow-well-met salutation “Yarvin, you reactionary fascist.” That was the same day The New York Times ran a discursive interview with Yarvin under the headline “Curtis Yarvin Says Democracy Is Done. Powerful Conservatives Are Listening.” Two of those, in addition to Vance, were Musk and Vought, who incorporated many of Yarvin’s schemes into Project 2025. “DOGE was one among many shocking triumphs for Thiel’s network in the second Trump era,” Durán writes.

For example, Yarvin had called for “a total shutdown of international relations, including security guarantees, foreign aid, and mass immigration,” all of which quickly became marquee policies of the Trump administration.

So here we are, less than halfway through a presidential administration already considered to be the most corrupt in US history. Much of that corruption has been facilitated by Silicon Valley elites who have helped Trump and his family make billions of dollars in exchange for the freedom to operate with little regulatory friction. Artificial intelligence companies, cryptocurrencies and crypto exchanges, prediction markets, and media conglomerates have all benefited. Palantir has obtained over $1 billion in government contracts from, among others, the Departments of Defense, Homeland Security, Energy, Transportation, Health and Human Services, Commerce, Agriculture, Transportation, and Veterans Affairs. Musk has cashed in prodigiously: an investigation by Senator Elizabeth Warren discovered more than a hundred ways Musk profited from his proximity to the Trump administration, including apparently getting Trump to fire the inspector general of USAID, who was investigating claims that Starlink had provided Internet services to Russia as it waged war against Ukraine. Less well-known players have also gotten in on the grift. A report from the top Democrat on the House Committee on the Judiciary, Jamie Raskin, found among other things that

the Trump Administration has intervened to halt or terminate federal investigations and enforcement actions involving multiple cryptocurrency firms that have donated to the President or invested in his companies…issued pardons and rolled back sanctions for known bad actors that have provided financial support to his ventures…[and] systematically dismantled anti-corruption and financial integrity safeguards.

Is it ideologically inconsistent that companies led by men who excoriate the federal government, profess a desire to see it dismantled, and lobby hard to skirt taxes are being enriched by our tax dollars through generous government contracts? It is not. When it comes down to it, their politics have always been motivated by the desire to amass as much money as possible; democracy is just an impediment. But cultivating the conditions for its demise takes time. A good first step is to install an executive who has no respect for the norms of democracy and prop him up with cronies who will defer to him. Is it any surprise that the largest donor in the 2026 midterm elections is Andreessen Horowitz? Again, it is not.

Money is power—that’s axiomatic. Gil Durán believes that “to create a better future, we must create a world without billionaires. We can have billionaires, or we can have democracy.” But here, I think, Durán overstates his case. He writes:

We do not allow private citizens to own nuclear weapons because such power does not belong in the hands of individuals…. A single nuke might kill hundreds of thousands of people, but the billionaires will kill millions or billions.

The problem is not that we live in a world with billionaires—it’s that we live in a world where a small coterie of billionaires with totalitarian aspirations have gotten so close to power. Durán is not wrong to repeat what have become “resistance” shibboleths—that we need to eliminate the influence of money in politics, institute real and effective regulation on artificial intelligence, cryptocurrency, and other dangerous technologies, and then, if these projects succeed, hold technofascists accountable for the damage they have done. These are all crucial.

In the short term, though, so is understanding to whom candidates vying for election in the midterms are beholden and how this support will determine their efforts to rein in hazardous technology—or not. Practicing democracy is the only way to preserve democracy. It is also a reminder that the dystopia celebrated by Thiel, Yarvin, Musk, and the tech bros in their thrall is not a given.

entries.content:
It was a time when fragments, lost poems, and early pages of unfinished manuscripts mattered. In 1938 the poet Antonio Machado, his mother, and his brother made their way from Spain to France to escape Franco’s advancing fascist forces. When Machado died in February 1939 in Collioure, his brother found in his pocket the first line of his last poem: “Those blue days, this childhood sun.”

In 1942, when the poet Miguel Hernández died in prison, where he had languished after the Spanish Civil War, he left a body of work that was later published as Cancionero y romancero de ausencias (Songs and Ballads of Absence, 1958). Some of his best-known poems were written on scraps of paper.

The most famous among these poets was Federico García Lorca, who was murdered by fascist soldiers near Granada in the south of Spain in August 1936. Lorca left much unpublished and half-finished work, both poems and plays. “The state of his manuscripts,” Leslie Stainton writes in Lorca: A Dream of Life (1999),

demonstrates the extent to which the act and art of creation were a part of his everyday life. He wrote poems on invitations to tea, royalty statements, envelopes, and drawings…. [He] wrote plays on the backs of poems.

After the civil war, most of Lorca’s family moved to New York. Before departing, Sarah Arvio writes in the introduction to Poet in Spain (2017), her translation of his poems,

Federico’s father collected all the manuscripts he could find and handed them over to a banker who had been friends with both the poet and his brother, Francisco. The banker stowed them in a vault in the Banco Urquijo—on calle Alcalá in Madrid, the very street where the poet had lived.

Many of these manuscripts are now in the Fundación Federico García Lorca in Granada. Among them is a group of poems known as the “Sonnets of Dark Love,” which were not published until 1983. Arvio describes seeing them for the first time: “The most moving of all the manuscripts I saw is a draft of Dark Love Sonnets—the only draft in the poet’s hand known to exist.” The poems were written on “thin, grayish paper,” the notepaper of the Hotel Victoria in Valencia, where he stayed in November 1935. “All were rapidly written with a blunt pencil in the same hand—as though he had not paused from beginning to end.” She reports that “Neruda and others have said that Lorca was at work on the sonnets in spring and summer of 1936, in the months before his death; he toted them around in his pockets.” But no later versions have ever been found. Arvio writes that Lorca, at the time he wrote these poems, “was deeply in love; he wrote these ten superb sonnets to his absent beloved…in a hotel room.” The beloved she names as Rafael Rodríguez Rapún. (This, however, is open to dispute, since there is also a claim that the sonnets were dedicated to Juan Ramírez de Lucas, whom Lorca referred to as “el rubio de Albacete”—the blond from Albacete—and who later became an art critic.)

Ian Gibson in his groundbreaking Federico García Lorca: A Life (1989) explains why Rapún remains somewhat mysterious:

About Lorca and Rafael Rodríguez Rapún’s relationship at this time [the summer of 1935], it is almost impossible to obtain any information: no correspondence has come to light; there are no diaries, and oral information on the subject is as scant as it is unhelpful. All we can surmise is that, given their professional as well as affective relationship, the two must have been together virtually every day.

Rapún, born in Madrid in 1912, was fourteen years younger than Lorca. He was, Gibson writes, “of athletic build, a good footballer and passionate socialist.” Although he was studying engineering, he joined La Barraca, the traveling theater group with which Lorca was involved, and became its secretary in 1933. According to one friend whom Gibson interviewed, Rapún was not homosexual:

Rafael was crazy about women…but he got caught in the net, no, not caught, immersed in Federico…. He became immersed in the whole affair without realizing what was happening. Later he tried to get away but he couldn’t…. It was tremendous.

We have to be careful, however, with this account of Rapún, since many who later gave accounts of this period were uneasy about homosexuality. The other account of Rapún—from a colleague in La Barraca—refers to his “elemental” nature that caused him to have an automatic orgasm “when our van overtook another car on the road.”

Only one letter from Rapún to Lorca has come to light. Quoted in Gibson’s book, it was written in 1933 when Lorca was in Buenos Aires:

Advertisement

I remember you constantly. Not to be able to see a person with whom you have been every hour of the day for months is too much to be forgotten. Especially if towards the person in question you feel yourself drawn as strongly as I do towards you.

After Lorca’s death, Rapún took an artillery course and, with the rank of lieutenant, was commanding a battery near Reinosa south of Santander when there was an air attack. Gibson writes, “Unlike the other men Rapún did not throw himself to the ground but remained sitting on a parapet. A bomb exploded nearby and he was mortally wounded.” He died in a military hospital in Santander on August 18, 1937, precisely a year after Lorca’s murder, and was buried in a graveyard beside the Cantabrian Sea.

In La Bola Negra, a film directed by Javier Calvo and Javier Ambrossi that won the best director award at Cannes in May, Rapún, played by Miguel Bernardeau, is taken to the hospital in Santander, but he does not die there. Instead he is subsequently executed by firing squad in a field at the edge of the sea. The final shot is delivered by a young fascist soldier called Sebastián, played by the actor and singer known as Guitarricadelafuente.

We first see Sebastián as he prepares to play the trumpet in the opening scene of the film. The residents of a raggedy Spanish village are trying to show their loyalty to the fascist cause while they wait for Mussolini’s planes to fly over them. They are so eager that they are almost ridiculous. Sebastián seems to worry that his mother, by her absence, is not showing enough support for the cause. When she appears and puts her arm up in loyalty, the planes begin to strafe the villagers, mistaking them for the enemy; only Sebastián survives.

The problem is how to read this scene. Obviously it is sad and surprising, but on two viewings I found it oddly comic. This was partly because of Guitarricadelafuente’s portrayal of Sebastián. He is strangely vacant and endearingly gormless. He has the wrong haircut. As he tries to escape, he climbs on an oversize statue of the saint after whom he is named. That too has an absurd or exaggerated edge. Soon he is, as he says later, handed a rifle. He is put on a truck. He is now, as much as he can be, a full-fledged soldier on the fascist side.

He stands apart from his fellow soldiers throughout the rest of the film. He is uncomfortable; he peers; he gawks. They are a reasonably good-humored lot, many of them remarkably handsome, as though they were in a men’s cologne ad. There is a brilliant cabaret scene with Penélope Cruz in which they look like English troops from, say, World War I, smiling, innocent fellows on a night out. Since they are close to the ocean, they take off their uniforms and cavort naked in the water. They look good from behind and enjoy horseplay.

We get to view the other side—Republican troops—mostly when they are dead, as jumbled corpses in the back of a jeep. (This is one of the few moments that rupture the general avoidance of horror in the film.) In one of these jeeps, there is a man still alive. High-ranking fascist officers know that this soldier has seemed to want death, and they presume that he knows secrets and is concerned about being taken alive. They do not realize that he is Rafael Rodríguez Rapún and that he was Lorca’s lover.

Sebastián, who is detailed to guard him, is puzzled when his prisoner drops a piece of paper to the floor. It has a poem written on it, one of Lorca’s Sonnets of Dark Love: “The beloved sleeps on the poet’s breast.” Since Lorca did not make his homosexuality public, this poem is especially significant because in line two it uses the gendered word dormido, signifying that the beloved is a man.

The two often gaze at each other, Sebastián a bit more than Rapún. It is burgeoning love across the barricades. All the politics are taken out of the story, as is much of the sheer viciousness that characterized the war. The tone is light; it is brash; some of the material is farcical. The narrative deliberately, it seems, lacks weight and depth. It is extravagant, a kind of romp. It is hardly what we expect in a film about the fascist side in the Spanish Civil War. It says more, perhaps, about the period in which it was made than it does about the past. In King Lear, Gloucester says of his son Edmund, “There was good sport at his making.” The same feeling comes across in La Bola Negra: an infectious sense that the filmmakers had a good time putting it all together.
