The first time I heard someone say that the fascists in Spain should not be demonized was in 1988 at the unveiling of a statue in a suburb of Barcelona to commemorate the withdrawal of the International Brigades from the country, at which the Socialist mayor of Barcelona, Pasqual Maragall, spoke. Among his audience were many ex-members of the brigades, old soldiers. Maragall, speaking in Catalan and French and English, alluded to the need for reconciliation and to not humiliate the other side. In English, he said, “They too had their ideals.” This caused one old lefty to heckle him, but the rest sat in stunned silence.

That was almost forty years ago. But the debate about the civil war has not gone away. Earlier this year a controversy erupted over who had suffered most and who the victims were and who has the right to speak. David Uclés is a Spanish writer born in 1990. His third novel, La península de las casas vacías (The Peninsula of Empty Houses, 2024), which dramatizes the impact of the civil war on several generations of a family, has been a best seller in Spain and has won numerous prizes. Lorca appears in the book, as do Hemingway and Orwell. Earlier this year Uclés published La ciudad de las luces muertas (The City of Dead Lights), set immediately after the war, which won one of the main Spanish literary prizes and also became a best seller.

Soon after the appearance of La ciudad de las luces muertas, Uclés announced that he was withdrawing from a conference to be held in Seville entitled “1936: The War We All Lost,” partly because two right-wing politicians—former prime minister José María Aznar and one of the founders of the far-right party Vox—were among the participants, but also because of the title. “We didn’t all lose the war,” Uclés said. “We all suffered through it, but the Republicans lost it and the Francoists won it.” One of the organizers of the event, the writer Arturo Pérez-Reverte, responded:

Any fool knows there was a winning side in the Civil War, undoubtedly; but all Spaniards lost, as I said before, freedom, culture, lives, homes, families, futures, democracy. And the proof that we lost is that we are still entangled in this mess. Ninety years later. Of course, we lost, and what’s worse is that we continue to lose. And this is said by someone whose father, grandfather, and uncle fought for the Republic and suffered the consequences, especially my grandfather. So, I am authorized to speak about this.

What was notable about this debate was its sheer vehemence and urgency, as though who won the war and who lost had not been settled many years ago.

It may seem obvious that the civil war is still a haunting presence in Spain, but that is only partly true. It is also the case that the war is often viewed with complete indifference. For many, it is hardly worth thinking about. La Bola Negra is caught between these two versions of the past, which perhaps accounts for its untidiness, its mixture of pathos and bright spectacle, its bloated rhetoric, its tender moments, its indifference to historical accuracy, its fascination with the legacy of Lorca.

The films about the civil war in Spain that have come fitfully and sporadically since the death of Franco in 1975 have been overshadowed by the films of Pedro Almodóvar, whose production company, El Deseo, is among the producers of La Bola Negra. Soon after the death of the dictator, Almodóvar came up with the idea that the present moment—especially in Madrid—was of supreme interest. Families did not interest his characters much, nor did parents or religion or party politics or history. Sexual politics interested them, as did self-invention and interior decor. They replaced their families with their friends. They replaced the haunting legacy of the civil war with sudden bursts of quick wit and fierce desire. After two decades of filmmaking, Almodóvar seemed to have made a country in his own likeness. It was surprising, then, in 2021 to see his film Parallel Mothers, in which a photographer, played by Penélope Cruz, is haunted by mass graves from the civil war in her village and has an affair with a forensic anthropologist who is working to identify the bodies of victims of fascism.

The war is like a vampire that won’t stay dead. The question is: Can it still be represented in a single story, with a single protagonist and a clear outcome? Could the tone of a film about it ninety years later be subtle and ironic and wistful? La Bola Negra could easily have been a moving and melancholy film about the death of Lorca and the subsequent year in the life of Rapún. Instead it comes with a kind of exuberance that Almodóvar once applied to the present. It tells a story with three strands, moving with gusto between them. The first is set in 1937 as Rapún is captured and guarded by the hapless Sebastián. It is partly based on a play by Alberto Conejero, La piedra oscura (The Dark Stone, 2017). Conejero, along with the two directors, wrote the screenplay.

The second strand is based on a fragment of a play in Lorca’s archive called La bola negra, which takes up all of two pages in his Teatro completo. The first page gives a list of characters that includes twenty-year-old Carlos, his friends and family, and the members of an exclusive club. It also includes skiers and snow as characters. We are given no explanation for this. The dialogue we have is just one page, a short encounter between Carlos and his sister. Although Lorca’s plans for the work were expanded in a letter to a friend, La bola negra remained just a dream. The film fleshes out the drama around Carlos (played by Milo Quifes) as in 1934 he is refused membership in the club because of his homosexuality.

The third strand of the film is set in the Madrid of 2017. Alberto (played by Carlos González) is a young gay man and the grandson of Sebastián, who has recently died. Having abandoned playwriting, he is now doing research on music. His coked-up mother is out of control. There is a brilliant scene in a restaurant where, in a rage, she hurls abuse and dumps some food on him. He leads a kind of life that could easily be from an Almodóvar film. Indeed, Almodóvar is mentioned in a scene with Alberto and his friends.

Alberto’s grandfather, whom he never met, has left him something mysterious in his will. It turns out that Sebastián had in his possession all those years the full manuscript of the play La bola negra—minus the first four pages—which can now be performed.

The discovered manuscript also has to be shown to an American Lorca scholar, played superbly by Glenn Close with a magnificently wooden Spanish accent. When she realizes its significance, she can say “Cancel my flight” without any worry about cliché. The film is unembarrassed about cliché. The clichés come in battalions. As the end approaches, for example, Sebastián is given “one minute” by a fellow fascist soldier to be alone with Rapún. Some of the big bodega or cabaret scenes could come from a thousand earlier movies. When Carlos is forced to answer whether or not he is gay, the ceiling falls in on him, as it would. This use of cliché adds to the general sense of broad-stroked comedy verging on farce, exacerbated by the speed with which things happen and the many scene changes.

As Rapún is taken to be executed, Sebastián sits beside him in the back of the truck, putting his thigh close to Rapún’s, as if their affair were only starting. Rapún’s final moments are either desperately sad or almost ludicrous or a heady, melodramatic mixture of both. Alberto, eighty years later, is in a strange position: his grandfather shot Rapún; he was also, to some extent, in love with Rapún; he rescued and preserved an important Lorca manuscript; he was a gay man in Franco’s Spain. Alberto’s relationship to the past is thus vastly ambiguous. He seems puzzled when Rapún’s brother hangs up the phone on him. Like several others in the movie, he only wants to help.

On the matter of fascism and Franco, the film is notable for its lack of earnestness about what has been viewed up to now as a most tragic event. But there is one subject on which it is wholly earnest: gay freedom and sexual repression. Indeed, there are moments in the film when you could be at a progressive meeting about the gay future in some open-minded forum in present-day Madrid.

The war offers young Sebastián a slow sexual awakening. We learn that he spent most of his subsequent life in a satisfying gay relationship. His partner tells Alberto how happy Sebastián would be if he were to witness his grandson living openly with his boyfriend in Madrid.

The scenes with Carlos, inspired by Lorca’s fragment La bola negra, offer us a version of young Lorca, the gay scion of a respectable upper-middle-class family. The scene in which Carlos is blackballed by the club is heavily stylized, like a dream of Spanish repression before the war. The young man moves innocently and confidently in the streets. When, on his father’s advice, he returns to face the membership committee, he is asked directly if he is homosexual. Rather than a likely moment from 1934, this is closer to the kind of nightmare that threatened Lorca and eventually overtook him—that he would be ruined in the city that had nurtured him. But it is significant that it is not his politics that puts Carlos in danger but rather his sexuality.

In a black-and-white sequence, Lorca actually appears in the film, played by the theater director and performer Alberto Cortés. In these scenes, Cortés and Bernardeau bear an uncanny resemblance to the Lorca and Rapún we know from photographs. Cortés plays Lorca in an exquisitely mannered style. He is about to go to Granada, where he believes, wrongly, that he will be safe. Rapún is right to be concerned about him. The screenwriters have a chance here to let Lorca speak, find a tone for him. He was known as a great talker. What he mainly says is that he hopes that the lives of the next generation of gay people will be better.

La Bola Negra, then, distills the battles fought in Spain in the 1930s between fascism and democracy, between restriction and freedom, down to questions of sexuality. All the main characters are gay men—Sebastián, Carlos, Alberto, Rapún, and Lorca. Their search for freedom offers the film a tone that is glittering and flippant. The dark knowledge of what happened in the civil war is left throbbing in the background. It is as though the filmmakers sought release from the war’s grim embrace and came up with La Bola Negra as a brilliant and wayward distraction, slyly sidestepping the tragedy of what happened, creating an alternative panorama.

entries.title: Mapping Mississippi White
entries.summary: Bennie Thompson’s trailblazing career came after the success of the Voting Rights Act and could end with its fall.
entries.source: The New York Review of Books
entries.content:
When Congress passed the Voting Rights Act in 1965, Bennie Thompson was seventeen years old—short of the voting age—so his parents reaped its benefits before he did. The family lived in Bolton, Mississippi, a town of about five hundred people twenty miles west of Jackson. Thompson’s mother, a schoolteacher, and his father, an auto mechanic, had never been able to register and vote.

The VRA essentially put states with histories of racial discrimination into federal receivership to force them to comply with the Fifteenth Amendment’s guarantee that the right to vote could not be denied because of race. As a first step, the federal government sent workers to the South to register Black citizens like Thompson’s parents. To assure further compliance, Section 5 of the act required those states to get approval from the Justice Department or a court before making any changes to their electoral systems. The federal registrars “created an opportunity to get registered without intimidation,” Thompson told me recently as we wandered through Bolton, where he still lives. “And the result was people like Bennie Thompson.”

Thompson discovered politics in the mid-Sixties as a student at Tougaloo College, a historically Black school and a civil rights hotbed in Jackson. He graduated in 1968 and, thanks to the new voters enfranchised by the VRA, won local office in Bolton the following year. (Prior to 1965, roughly 28,500 Black citizens in Mississippi—6.7 percent of those eligible—were registered to vote; within two years of the act’s passage, that number had soared to 264,000—59.8 percent.) Over the next two decades Thompson won a series of races for county-level positions in Mississippi and then, in 1993, a special election to Congress. He’s been reelected sixteen times. Thompson and Mike Espy, his predecessor in the seat, are the only Black people to be elected to Congress in Mississippi since Reconstruction.

Thompson has been the chair and ranking member of the House Committee on Homeland Security, but he came to broad national attention when then speaker Nancy Pelosi named him the chair of the special congressional committee charged with investigating the riot at the Capitol on January 6, 2021. In a series of televised hearings in 2022, Thompson’s committee laid out how a violent insurrection nearly upended the transfer of presidential power. “I named a lot of our most intelligent and skilled members to that committee,” Pelosi told me.

And you know how Congress is. They all thought they should be the chairman. But after it was over, they all came to me and said that Bennie was so fair and showed so much integrity and skill that they agreed that he was the right one to be the chair.

Thompson has lived his entire political life in the shadow—and, for a long time, under the protection—of the VRA. Throughout that period, Congress and the courts have wrestled with a central question about its meaning, one with fundamental implications for Thompson’s political career. Does the VRA protect Black voters and officeholders only from intentional discrimination by government officials, or does it also guarantee Black candidates a fair chance of victory at the polls? To put the question in voting rights shorthand, is it an “intent” law or a “results” law?

Earlier this year the Supreme Court appeared to settle the question. In Louisiana v. Callais, a 6–3 majority in effect established that the VRA prohibited only intentional discrimination. Republican-dominated states throughout the country, including Mississippi, took the decision as an invitation to gerrymander the seats of Black officeholders so they would have virtually no chance of winning reelection. Just two weeks after Callais was decided, Tate Reeves, the Republican governor of Mississippi, announced his intention to redraw the lines of Thompson’s district. “Congressman Bennie G. Thompson’s reign of terror on MS-2 is over,” Reeves posted on social media. “It is not a matter of ‘IF…’ Just a matter of ‘WHEN!’” The governor’s inflammatory language is revealing, especially because Thompson has had a scandal-free career; the only “terror” about Thompson, it seems, is that he’s Black and in Congress. While Reeves and his Republican allies in the state legislature ultimately decided against a new round of gerrymandering before the 2026 midterms, they are united in their determination to redraw not only Thompson’s district, but also those of Black officeholders in state and local positions across the state.

If the governor does end Thompson’s congressional career, it will mark more than the conclusion of a single politician’s time in office. It will signal the end of a grand experiment: a joint undertaking of the federal government and the courts to rectify enduring injustices in the American electoral system. More than half a century ago, the nearly absolute power wielded by white politicians in the South created the need for the VRA. Now, as a result of Callais and other Supreme Court decisions, the heirs to those politicians are reclaiming that power.

Advertisement

“Just to mention Mississippi, to cross the state line from Alabama and go there, it just created all types of problems in my own mind,” John Lewis once said, recalling his early days as a civil rights leader. “Alabama is bad; Alabama is hell. But to go to Mississippi at the time was worse than hell.”1

In Mississippi in the 1960s, racist violence was a horrible constant. In 1963 Medgar Evers, the first field officer of the NAACP in the state, was shot dead in the driveway of his house in Jackson. The following year, when caravans of students and others came to register voters during the Freedom Summer, their buses were torched and the passengers beaten. Three of them—James Chaney, Andrew Goodman, and Michael Schwerner—were abducted and murdered by the Ku Klux Klan.

This was the Mississippi where Bennie Thompson grew up. In the months after the VRA was passed, there were two cross burnings in Bolton. As he took me through its streets, Thompson showed me the United Methodist church he first went to as a child. “I’ve been in one physical church my whole life. Not just one religion, one physical church—which just happened to be right next door to the Head Start center that the Klan burned down,” he told me. “So that was kind of part of my introduction.”

The Supreme Court purported to end segregation in public schools in Brown v. Board of Education in 1954, but a decade later, Thompson was taught in what was still called the Bolton Colored School, which it was in fact if not in law. Most of Bolton’s white children eventually went to a private school called Central Hinds Academy just outside town. We took a drive to Central Hinds and happened on a football practice that featured, by my count, about two dozen white kids and one Black player. Thompson smiled and gestured at the lone figure: “He’s an athlete.”

A short distance from Bolton’s main drag, which has just a handful of storefronts, Thompson slowed down in front of a modest swimming pool. When he became mayor of Bolton in 1973, he learned that the town had donated $2,500 to the local nonprofit that had built the pool a few years earlier and then decreed that it was whites only. “My position was, the public money was donated, therefore, it’s a public pool,” he told me. “I closed the pool and said unless you make it a public pool, you can’t open.” In response, the nonprofit simply refunded the town’s $2,500: “They kept it all white.” (The pool is now in private hands.)

Meanwhile, the white politicians in charge of the Mississippi state government fought the VRA in every way they could. The local authorities could no longer stop Black citizens from registering, but the state had many other tools to preserve white rule. In 1966 the state legislature gerrymandered the state’s congressional districts so that Black voters in the Mississippi Delta region were split among three districts and were thus powerless to elect one of their own. (Then as now, Mississippi has the highest percentage of Black residents of any state: about 40 percent then and about 37 percent now.) The state also rewrote the rules in many white-majority cities and towns so that officials were elected at-large rather than by neighborhood, which might have given Black candidates a chance. In eleven communities, the state changed school superintendent positions from elected to appointed to prevent Black candidates from running and winning.

Some of those changes were challenged by the federal government. The early years of the VRA, when Thompson came of age, unfolded in a national political environment very different from today’s. The law enjoyed bipartisan support. Even though Richard Nixon embraced the “Southern Strategy,” playing to white racism in the South to win the presidency in 1968, he signed a reauthorization of the VRA in 1970; Gerald Ford did the same in 1975. During the administrations of these Republican presidents, the Justice Department used its authority under Section 5 of the VRA to veto some of the attempts by Mississippi and other states to thwart the intent of the law.

Still, progress for Black Mississippians often came slowly, including for Thompson. When the VRA was passed, Black residents were in the majority in two of the five supervisors’ districts in Hinds County, which includes Jackson. But county officials changed the election for supervisors to an at-large system. Black voters sued, and eventually, in 1977, the full Fifth Circuit declared that Hinds County violated the VRA. As Frank R. Parker, the lawyer for the plaintiffs, wrote in his book Black Votes Count (1990),

The board of supervisors was forced to adopt a new plan that contained two districts that were over 65 percent black. In the 1979 county elections—after eight years of litigation—two black county supervisors, Bennie G. Thompson and George Smith, were elected as the first black county supervisors in Hinds County since Reconstruction.

Whenever the subject of race and voting in Mississippi came up, Thompson always offered the same straightforward explanation: “If you look at the historical voting patterns, especially in the South, Black people vote for white and Black candidates, but for the most part, white voters still vote for white candidates.” To Thompson, enforcement of the VRA must take those facts into consideration or the law would have no meaning at all. If states are allowed to gerrymander legislative districts so that Black candidates have no chance of winning—regardless of what could be proved about the legislators’ racial intentions—then white domination of the political process would continue as before 1965. Still, in the early versions of the VRA, the text was ambiguous about whether it was an “intent” or a “results” law.

Advertisement

The Supreme Court offered an initial answer in City of Mobile v. Bolden (1980). According to the Court, it was not enough if Black voters failed to elect one of their own; they had to prove that the white majority intended to violate their voting rights. Civil rights supporters denounced the Mobile decision, asserting that in the modern era, white legislators knew better than to display racially discriminatory intent. Proving again the bipartisan support for voting rights at the time, Republicans and Democrats joined forces in 1982 to pass a twenty-five-year extension of the VRA that was revised to effectively overturn the Mobile decision. Conservative senators like Orrin Hatch and Robert Dole voted for the extension, and Ronald Reagan signed it into law. It established a “results” test: plaintiffs needed to show only that a state’s action produced discriminatory outcomes in order to win their cases.

Again, Thompson owed the next step in his career to the VRA. After the 1982 changes to the act, Black plaintiffs challenged the 1966 gerrymander of the state’s congressional districts. Now they had to prove only that the creation of the districts led to discriminatory results, which they did. The courts compelled the state at last to establish a majority-Black congressional district, and Mike Espy won the seat in 1986. In 1993 President Bill Clinton appointed him secretary of agriculture. In the special election to fill the vacancy that year, Thompson won.

By this point, even though the makeup of the Supreme Court was almost the same, the justices had changed course on voting rights. In Thornburg v. Gingles (1986), they ratified—and strengthened—the results test established in the revision of the VRA by holding that states had to acknowledge when they had a history of “racially polarized voting.” In establishing district lines, they had to consider “whether whites vote sufficiently as a bloc usually to defeat the minority’s preferred candidate.” If white residents did vote that way, the states had to include enough Black voters to give a Black candidate a chance to win election. In other words, the Court recognized what Thompson told me about voters in Mississippi, and it thus ensured that districts like his would remain intact.

It’s now clear that the crucial event in the eventual demise of the VRA was President George W. Bush’s appointment in 2005 of John G. Roberts Jr. as chief justice. In the early 1980s, after Roberts had completed his clerkship with then associate justice William H. Rehnquist, he took a number of junior positions in President Reagan’s White House and Justice Department. There, in a series of memos, Roberts expressed his opposition to what became the 1982 reauthorization of the VRA. In strong language for a young staffer, Roberts endorsed the Court’s decision in the Mobile case and voiced his passionate belief that the law should protect Black voters only from intentional discrimination, not from unfair results. For example, in a January 26, 1982, memo to Attorney General William French Smith, he wrote that adding a results test to the law would lead to a “quota system in electoral politics.”

Roberts lost that battle, but his appointment to the Supreme Court put him in a position to win the war, especially once he was joined by other conservative justices. To Roberts and the other conservatives, the VRA was another way the government sought to privilege Black citizens over others, much like affirmative action, which they also eventually outlawed. Combining a narrow reading of the rights of Black voters under the VRA with an expansive understanding of the rights of whites under the Constitution, the conservatives began chipping away at the act.

The first great blow came in 2013 in Shelby County v. Holder, in which Roberts’s opinion for the Court effectively overruled Sections 4 and 5. In both the original version of the VRA and in every subsequent reauthorization, Congress held investigatory hearings and, based on the results, established a formula for determining which states and localities had histories of discrimination and thus were subject to the act’s provisions. The theme of Roberts’s opinion, however, was that the nation had changed. He wrote that after the passage of the VRA, “voting tests were abolished, disparities in voter registration and turnout due to race were erased, and African-Americans attained political office in record numbers.” The statutory formula did not, in his view, take these changes sufficiently into account, even though Congress had looked at the same facts and concluded otherwise. According to Roberts, the law violated “the tradition of equal sovereignty” among the states and was thus unconstitutional. Unless Congress changed the formula (which it was unlikely to do and never has), there would be no more jurisdictions subject to Section 5, which was now a dead letter.

Immediately after the Shelby County decision, several states formerly covered by Section 5, now freed from Justice Department oversight, changed their election laws to make it harder for Black people (and others) to vote. On the very day that the decision was announced, the Texas legislature announced that it would tighten the photo ID requirements for voting, which a court had earlier said burdened minorities. Mississippi and Alabama passed similar laws. North Carolina enacted a series of voter restriction measures, including a requirement of a government-issued ID, and a limitation on early voting. As a result of the Supreme Court’s decision, none of these changes had to be submitted to the Justice Department for preclearance. The southern states immediately showed that they had changed less than Roberts claimed they had.

In theory, Shelby County left open the kind of VRA lawsuits that made Thompson’s career possible. Under Section 2 of the law, individual plaintiffs, not just the federal government, could sue localities for violating the rights of Black voters. It was private Section 2 lawsuits during the Sixties and Seventies that forced Mississippi to reverse the gerrymandering that had ruled out Black candidates like Thompson for the Hinds County seats and his congressional district. But in the past few years the Supreme Court has shut down Section 2 lawsuits, too. And crucially the Court in 2019 allowed state legislatures to design districts that gave an advantage to a ruling party, holding in Rucho v. Common Cause that partisan gerrymandering is a “political question” beyond the remit of federal courts. The decision gave Republican map drawers in the South the perfect way to avoid being accused of racial discrimination. They could eliminate the seats of Black officeholders on the grounds that they were targeting only Democrats.

The coup de grâce came earlier this year, when the Court decided Callais, which made Roberts’s memos from the early 1980s the law of the land.2 Samuel Alito’s opinion for the Court said that its purpose was to “update the Gingles framework and realign it with the text of §2 and constitutional principles,” but the effect of the ruling was to overrule Gingles and invalidate the results test entirely. Citing Rucho, Alito said that henceforth “litigants cannot circumvent that rule by dressing their political-gerrymandering claims in racial garb.” But the truth was that he was inviting Republican state legislators to dress their racial gerrymandering in political garb, with likely fatal political consequences for Black officeholders like Thompson. As Justice Elena Kagan put it in her dissent, Callais was the “latest chapter in the majority’s now-completed demolition of the Voting Rights Act.”

In taking up the Supreme Court’s invitation in Callais, Governor Reeves and the Republican-dominated state legislature in Mississippi are proceeding in an orderly fashion. State legislative elections take place there in 2027, and the Republicans are moving first to gerrymander those seats to the advantage of Republican, and thus mostly white, candidates. According to an analysis of prospective maps by Fair Fight Action/Black Voters Matter, a liberal advocacy group, an aggressive post-Callais map by Republicans could eliminate twenty-nine—nearly half—of Mississippi’s Black-majority legislative districts. When that task is complete, Reeves and his colleagues will turn to congressional maps and the fate of Thompson’s district in 2028. Other longtime African American members of Congress, including Emanuel Cleaver in Missouri, James Clyburn in South Carolina, and Sanford Bishop in Georgia, are similarly at risk of losing their seats in 2028. In all, in the next two years, the Congressional Black Caucus, which began the current Congress with sixty-two members, could lose as many as nineteen because of the kind of redistricting now permitted by the Supreme Court.

In addition to his security responsibilities in Congress, Thompson also serves as a custodian of institutional memory of the civil rights movement. For the past twenty-seven years, he has hosted an annual Mississippi Policy Conference, sponsored by the Congressional Black Caucus, at which he introduces colleagues of all races and backgrounds to a part of the world they may not know and a history they may not remember. “I take folks and show them what cotton looks like growing in the field,” he told me. “I mean, some folks think cotton comes from Walmart.” The conference takes place in Tunica, which Robert Kennedy toured in 1967 when it was known as perhaps the poorest city in America. (The town’s fortunes have improved since the opening of a nearby casino.)

“I had never been to Mississippi before Bennie invited me to the conference,” Joe Neguse, a four-term congressman from Colorado, told me. Neguse, who is forty-two, belongs to a generation of Black politicians whose experiences differ greatly from Thompson’s. “It was one thing to read about what happened in Mississippi,” he said, “but it was another to go there and learn from Bennie and others who had to grapple with such obstacles.”

For now Thompson will campaign as usual in his so-far-unchanged district. He is cautiously optimistic about the future, too, pointing out to me that breaking up his district, which is roughly 64 percent Black, might involve some peril for the Republicans: “The $64,000 question for the Republican leadership in this state is, what are you going to do with the Black people? You gonna push them in the Mississippi River?”

To change Thompson’s district, the mapmakers would have to move its Black voters into the three other districts, which are all currently represented by white Republicans. That might give Democrats chances to win those seats: “So ultimately, you could create two purple districts and end up with two Democrats rather than one.” Republicans might not want to take that chance and thus might leave Thompson’s district more or less intact. (There’s also a chance that Thompson might not run again in 2028.)

Given the number of Black voters in Mississippi, it will not be easy for Republican state legislators to gerrymander every one of their districts into oblivion, but the party is clearly going to try. The tools to fight back are very different today from what they were in the first decades after the passage of the VRA. Even if the Justice Department were inclined to protect the gains of Black voters and officeholders (which it clearly is not under the Trump administration), the Supreme Court’s invalidation of Section 5 has made such an effort impossible. And the Court itself, which was at least sometimes an ally of the VRA, has turned into an implacable foe. As a result, there will soon be fewer Black elected officials, perhaps a lot fewer, than there have been in the recent past. Representative democracy will look, and be, less representative, which is the problem that gave rise to the VRA.

“The issue is not whether Bennie Thompson represents this district or not,” Thompson said. “It’s whether or not the people who live in this district have a shot at representing and electing the candidates of their choice.”

entries.title: Vermeer’s Vanishing Act
entries.summary: Why is it that so many smart, inquisitive writers, smitten by the elusiveness of Vermeer’s pictures, should work so hard to wrestle that elusiveness into submission?
entries.source: The New York Review of Books
entries.content:
One of the many clever strokes in Andrew O’Hagan’s 2024 novel Caledonian Road was casting his floundering, public intellectual hero as the author of a best-selling biography of Johannes Vermeer. Given the paucity of facts about Vermeer’s life and the thoroughness with which that paucity has been picked over, knowledgeable readers may have sniffed, but the joke is on the sniffers, since the fictional biography is pointedly a book about an absent subject—an outline around essential emptiness. (Needless to say, there’s a metaphor there.)

The biography’s success nets its author lucrative gigs with fashion houses, which should be preposterous, but the current state of real-world Vermeer fandom makes it believable. Three years after the Rijksmuseum exhibition broke the box office (not a metaphor—the ticketing system collapsed under the demand), you can buy skateboards blazoned with Girl with a Pearl Earring, bathe with rubber ducks sporting her turban, or (like a woman I recently saw sketching at Tate Britain) have her face tattooed on your bicep. At the more cerebral end of the market, recent months have seen the publication of Closer to Vermeer, a Rijksmuseum compendium of serious research papers in the guise of a lovely coffee table book; Vermeer’s Afterlives, Ruth Bernard Yeazell’s account of the painter’s effect on artists and writers from Proust to Richter; and yes, an ambitious new biography, Vermeer: A Life Lost and Found, by the well-known British art historian and broadcaster Andrew Graham-Dixon.

What is it about Vermeer? There are plenty of other entrancing Dutch Golden Age painters out there: Pieter de Hooch’s playful children are backlit delights; Caspar Netscher’s The Lace Maker is a miracle of quiet concentration. There’s Rembrandt, for goodness’ sake. But nobody is selling baseball caps with Netscher’s Lace Maker on them. And nobody carries on about a Sphinx of Leiden or The Hague or Amsterdam the way they do about the Sphinx of Delft.

The magic of Vermeer resides in the paintings—their peculiar way of being at once sociable and silent, of making the fall of light feel both transcendent and palpable. But the mystique of Vermeer—the sphinxiness first ascribed to him in 1858 by the French critic Théophile Thoré-Bürger—has much to do with the two centuries of obscurity between his death in 1675 and his rediscovery. Having come upon the View of Delft in The Hague’s Mauritshuis while in political exile from his native France, Thoré-Bürger adopted the role of obsessive detective, seeking to learn who the artist was and what else he had made: “To see one picture by van der Meer, I traveled hundreds of miles: to obtain a photograph of another van der Meer, I was madly extravagant.” Yeazell opens her book with his claim “This Vermeer has driven us crazy. But we have revived him.”

Most of those rediscovered Vermeers were hiding in plain sight but misattributed to other artists. One critical clue in sorting this out was the 1696 auction listing of twenty-one paintings by “J. vander Meer van Delft” from the estate of a man named Jacob Dissius. Some of its terse descriptions were easily paired to known works (“the town of Delft seen in perspective from the south”). Some were less helpful (“a view of some house”), and a couple have never found a match. (If you should happen upon a seventeenth-century canvas of “a gentleman washing his hands, in a perspectival room, with figures, artful and rare,” contact the authorities.)

Thoré-Bürger was overly optimistic in many of his attributions, but he was right enough to provide modern audiences with a first sense of Vermeer not merely as the equal of better-remembered peers but as qualitatively distinct. Abjuring the shadowy drama of Rembrandt, the slapstick of Jan Steen, and the coziness of de Hooch, Vermeer’s pictures were quietly perplexing—the action stilled, the narratives incomplete. Many genre paintings look like freeze-frames from a stage play—the actors explicit in their gestures, comedic attitudes, or shows of affection. Vermeer’s always seem to be waiting for their lines.

His disregard for obvious plots was, Yeazell points out, one of the things that made Vermeer feel “modern” in the late nineteenth century. To artists disenchanted with the narrative drudgery of academic painting, Vermeer’s preference for seemingly ordinary moments resonated, as did his fascination with light and his sometimes abrupt brushwork. Connections were drawn between Vermeer and Impressionism, Vermeer and Whistler, Vermeer and Manet. People took note of what looked like proto-photographic effects in certain paintings—the oversize glints on reflective surfaces, the perceptually strange foreshortening, the way things move in and out of focus—as with the pile of red threads in the foreground of Vermeer’s The Lacemaker, which verges on abstraction. Yeazell cites W. Somerset Maugham’s alter ego in Of Human Bondage (1915), Philip Carey, pronouncing Vermeer “the one old master who painted like a modern.”

Advertisement

She also documents a lesser-known “generational phenomenon” of painters who took Vermeer as a model for retreat from the modern world. The clothing worn by their female subjects might be contemporary, but their activities might be seventeenth century: reading, sewing, fingering keyboards in beautifully lit rooms. The American Impressionist Thomas Dewing collected Vermeerish props like a chair with lion’s-head finials; others arranged antique crockery or piled textiles on foreground tables. Of telephones, radios, or electric lights, however, there is no sign, and the pictures feel not so much transcendent as claustrophobic. The Danes Vilhelm Hammershøi and Peter Ilsted engaged in less interior decor cosplay but convey their own airless Nordic noir.

What is interesting about these works is how they illuminate the original. Their preference for stasis, for example, makes one notice Vermeer’s gift for incipient action—the look of a decision about to be made, an event about to happen. We are alerted to the way he seems to discover the world afresh on every canvas, rather than reshaping it as something already seen on a museum wall. (One great exception, Yeazell points out, is Gerhard Richter’s effulgent portrait of his wife reading. Richter acknowledges longing to paint like Vermeer, but here as elsewhere he was seeking his own new answers to the question of how looking works.)

By the mid-twentieth century, Vermeer was enough of a trope that imitation was beside the point. For Joseph Cornell, placing a cutout of Girl with a Pearl Earring in his 1952 box Grand Hôtel Bon Port was a way of talking about longing and loss. For Salvador Dalí, painting a copy of Vermeer’s Lacemaker from large reproductions propped in the rhino enclosure of a zoo was a way of talking about Dalí. Filmmakers quoted Vermeer’s fall of light as a way to still time. Novelists worked to fill his seductive silences with servant girl romances and encrypted desire. Poets attached themselves in such numbers that Jane Shore titled a 2023 poem “I Am Sick of Reading Poems About Paintings by Vermeer.”

Art historians too were keen to make Vermeer their own. Yeazell takes us on a tour of the many academic trends that have been brought to bear, beginning with the connoisseurship required to distinguish Vermeers from not-Vermeers. (One chapter is given over to the Han van Meegeren forgeries, connoisseurship’s great comeuppance.) Having largely solved the question of what Vermeer painted, scholars turned to the question of what he meant.

Iconographers analyzed the maps and paintings in his pictures for covert messages; they scoured Dutch emblem books (printed compilations of moralizing memes) for signposts his original audience might have recognized. But endless questions remained: Was the presence of a map predating the Dutch Republic a political gesture, and if so, pro or con? Was the girl smiling demurely at a soldier an image of vice or virtue? And what on earth was up with the eye-rolling, snake-squishing, breast-clutching woman in Allegory of the Catholic Faith? Researchers have now examined the economy in which Vermeer operated, the sources of his pigments, the behavior of his sociopathic brother-in-law, the interior layouts of the buildings he might have called home. Yet 394 years after his (Protestant) baptism, Johannes Vermeer of Delft remains an enigma wrapped in a slit-sleeve doublet (if indeed the fancy-pants guy with his back to us in The Art of Painting is a self-effacing self-portrait, as many believe).

Maddeningly—or conveniently, depending on your agenda—the original documents in the case are few and far between: we have records of his baptism, his marriage, his guild membership, his death, and the financial difficulties faced by his widow and eleven surviving children. We know he was admired in his lifetime thanks to mentions by a couple of art-savvy travelers to Delft and a poem naming him as a phoenix risen from the ashes of the gunpowder magazine explosion that killed the painter Carel Fabritius. But we have no writings from his hand, no drawings, no account of his training. We don’t know his personality, his politics, or his religious leanings. Baptized in the Dutch Reformed church, he married into a Catholic family, lived a few doors down from a Jesuit mission, and left behind children with names like Ignatius and Franciscus.

Such slim biographical pickings are not unusual. John Michael Montias, the Yale economist whose research in the 1970s and 1980s did much to reconstruct the world around the artist, observed that lasting records usually involve brushes with authority—births, deaths, criminal proceedings. Graham-Dixon, who previously wrote a well-received biography of the brawling, homicidal Caravaggio, describes Vermeer’s thin file as the price of a “peaceable and law-abiding life.” But in this case, the sparseness of the evidence has combined with the ambiguity of the pictures to produce a persistent faith that somewhere there is a secret key that will unlock them both.

Advertisement

In 2001 Philip Steadman’s Vermeer’s Camera: Uncovering the Truth Behind the Masterpieces argued that Vermeer used a closet-size camera obscura to compose many of his interior paintings. In 2009 Benjamin Binstock’s Vermeer’s Family Secrets: Genius, Discovery, and the Unknown Apprentice dismissed the iconographers and “camera literalists,” and instead saw the pictures as enacting familial dramas and proposed that up to a sixth of the artist’s oeuvre was actually the work of his oldest daughter. Since family members, unlike apprentices, were not registered with the guild, she could have trained with and assisted her father while leaving no record. More recently (and less sensationally) the Rijksmuseum curator Gregor J.M. Weber’s Johannes Vermeer: Faith, Light and Reflection proposed that Vermeer had been not a Catholic convert of convenience, as many have suggested, but a true believer, and speculated that he may have encountered (or even acquired) a desktop camera obscura through the Jesuits down the block.

None of these theories has proved transformative, though bits and pieces of them have become accepted. Many specialists think it possible that Vermeer witnessed some form of projected images and was entranced enough to imitate the effect, but inventories show no such equipment in his possession, and experiments reported in Closer to Vermeer show that seventeenth-century lenses weren’t up to the task Steadman proposed. In 2022 new scientific analyses prompted the National Gallery in Washington, D.C., to downgrade its peculiar Girl with a Flute to “studio of Johannes Vermeer,” lending potential support to Binstock’s claim of familial authorship. But the Rijksmuseum still maintains that Flute is from the master’s own hand (albeit on a bad day), and no other paintings have been shown to share the oddities that called Flute into question.

For those with a taste for such things, the scientific papers in Closer to Vermeer are an enjoyable antidote to the full-throttle imaginings of much Vermeer literature. Conservators are by nature conservative: they explain the wondrous analytic abilities of the tools at their disposal—an alphabet soup of imaging tech (MA-XRF, MA-XRPD, RIS, FTIR, GC-MS)—and the limitations of those tools. They qualify their deductions with care. Computer-assisted weave maps of Vermeer canvases, for example, can tell us which paintings were cut from the same cloth and even where on the bolt the cut was made. They can suggest (not prove) which paintings may have been (not were) made around the same time. Refreshingly, the authors infer from this not a whit of personal meaning.

Andrew Graham-Dixon is not a conservator but a historian with a gift for making serious art accessible without dumbing it down. He is also the latest in the Thoré-Bürger mode to be driven crazy by Vermeer and to claim to have resurrected him in new ways. Promising a “disconcertingly new” account of the artist’s life, art, and intentions, his book turns on the biggest oddity in Vermeer’s paper trail: that roughly half of Vermeer’s estimated lifetime output belonged to a single family. Montias discovered that Jacob Dissius (the owner of those twenty-one auctioned works) was the son-in-law of a Delft couple, Pieter van Ruijven and Maria de Knuijt, who knew Vermeer. It now seems clear that Maria was the force behind their art collection (her will referred to “my” paintings, not “ours”) and was thus “the only person in the seventeenth-century Dutch Republic who is known to have collected half of any artist’s oeuvre,” Piet Bakker and Judith Noorman write in Closer to Vermeer. Maria also arranged to leave the painter a bequest, a stipulation for which Montias could find no precedent.

What was behind this singular relationship? To reach his answer Graham-Dixon takes us back to the founding of the Protestant Dutch Republic, some fifty years before Vermeer was born. A novel political experiment (which most of Europe assumed would fail), it was the result of rebellion against decades of brutal Spanish rule during which Dutch civilians were repeatedly massacred for their politics, religious convictions, or mere presence in the wrong town. The republic’s own internal struggles could also turn bloody, but on questions of religious orthodoxy the state blew hot and cold. The only legally sanctioned church was Dutch Reformed, but other faiths were tolerated in a typically Dutch way: their places of worship could not advertise—no spires or bell towers—though they might be substantial buildings. (Delft’s “hidden” Jesuit church could seat seven hundred.) There were Catholics, Lutherans, and Mennonites, there were Remonstrants, who denied predestination and held that salvation could be secured through faith and good deeds, and there were the leaderless Collegiants, a big tent movement in which Spinozan rationalism jostled with mystical modes, violence was condemned, even Catholics were welcome, and women’s voices were valued as much as men’s. (It is a testament to Graham-Dixon’s skills as a writer that he manages to make all this not only comprehensible but interesting.)

Having laid the ground, Graham-Dixon builds a case for Vermeer family connections to the Remonstrants: the painter’s mother had worked for a family related to the movement’s founder; a younger member of that family later loaned Vermeer money. For a while Vermeer’s parents lived close to the local Remonstrant preacher Johannes Taurinus, for whom the painter might have been named. (The highfalutin “Johannes” was an outlier in a world full of simple “Jans.”) Graham-Dixon then does the same for Vermeer’s patrons, identifying Remonstrant sympathies in the Van Ruijven family tree and arguing that de Knuijt at least was involved with the still more radical Collegiants.

For proof he has to lean on some pretty slim reeds (that the Van Ruijvens chose a notary whose first cousin was the foremost Collegiant; that Vermeer’s painting The Little Street may show the edge of the Van Ruijven house and a Remonstrant church behind it). But slim reeds are pretty much all we have with Vermeer, and Graham-Dixon weaves them together artfully to support his theory that not only did painter and patron share the same religious beliefs, but—drumroll here—the paintings Vermeer provided de Knuijt were designed for, and employed in, Collegiant worship. Vermeer’s Woman with a Balance? A depiction of private spiritual contemplation. The Milkmaid? An instance of the evangelical life, offering physical and spiritual succor. A Maid Asleep? A portrait of de Knuijt experiencing a religious vision (“Has the spirit of the Lord dwelt with her and held communion with her?” he asks). Like others before him, Graham-Dixon sees God in Vermeer’s light: what looks like filtered sunshine is actually “the indwelling light of the soul.”

The line he draws between Collegiant thought and Vermeer feels right. Looking at the rapt expression of Woman with a Pearl Necklace, one can easily imagine her listening to the still, small voice of the eternal. When he writes about the peaceful Apocalypse imagined by some Collegiants—an earthly paradise that might “sneak up on the world without the world noticing”—Vermeer’s pictures flood to mind. It is appealing to think that this most tender and attentive of painters chose a creed that valued peace over conflict, saw women and men as equals, and had faith in the possibility of transcendence right here, in the world of tables and chairs and plain plaster walls.

For a hundred years, Vermeer has been to art history what the Mirror of Erised was to young wizards at Hogwarts, showing each viewer what he or she longs to see. Thoré-Bürger, in exile from an autocratic emperor, discovered a master of “l’art pour l’homme.” Vermeer’s turn-of-the-century imitators found serene distance from a jangly new technological world. Steadman, a postwar architect, saw a technologically curious experimentalist. And now, as venality and performative violence deform our institutions and ethics, Graham-Dixon recognizes Vermeer as “one of a chosen few who built the values on which a tolerant and liberal civilization, our own even, might be based.”

Precisely because the theory suits so neatly our current needs, a little skepticism is in order. How much weight can Graham-Dixon’s data points bear? If you read fast enough, you might be able to whiz, Roadrunner style, over the gaps in the record, but as the book progresses it’s hard not to notice how quickly suppositions become facts onto which further suppositions are stacked. Eventually the argument starts to feel like a cross between a Jenga tower and a Möbius strip. Since there is no solid documentation for de Knuijt’s religious behavior, “Maria’s Collegiant activities must be inferred from the internal evidence of Vermeer’s paintings.” And since there are no known Collegiant paintings, the Collegiant pictorial agenda is derived from the Vermeer paintings.

“In almost no case,” Graham-Dixon warns us, “does my account of a given picture match up with anything previously written about it.” Those accounts go from fairly persuasive (the sky in View of Delft is numinous enough to double as the kingdom of heaven), to maybe if you squint (the spiritual reckoning of Maid Asleep), to bizarre. “We know the lacemaker is pregnant,” he claims, because the out-of-focus pile of red threads in the foreground is actually “the image of a woman’s womb, veins and arteries pulsing with blood.” (While there is a naughty Dutch pun to do with pin cushions, the threads-as-uterus idea indeed has no precedent.)

His hottest take is the identification of Girl with a Pearl Earring as a portrait of Vermeer’s patrons’ twelve-year-old daughter, Magdalena (later the wife of Jacob Dissius), in the guise of Mary Magdalene. The famously enigmatic expression that greets the viewer is, he explains, that of the Magdalene in the moment before recognizing Jesus risen from the tomb. Vermeer-heads are likely to object on two grounds: first, the picture was described as a tronie (an anonymous face) in the Dissius sale—an odd error if it depicted Dissius’s wife; and second, treating the viewer as a stand-in for the resurrected Christ seems theologically dicey.

This is nitpicky stuff, however, compared with the contradictions at the heart of his story. Many observers have assumed that, having married a Catholic bride in a Catholic church and lived with her and their Catholic children in a Catholic neighborhood, Vermeer had converted, either out of love or conviction. Graham-Dixon’s Vermeer, however, seems to despise the Catholic faith—in one passage the painter is imagined making works for his mother-in-law’s kitchen chapel “through gritted teeth.” The man who, we are told, embraced a faith based on tolerance and honesty is thus also a man who lived his life (and took vows) with fingers crossed behind his back. And while Graham-Dixon is not the first to depict Vermeer’s mother-in-law as a controlling harridan (though she seems to have supported the painter and his brood), he further works to separate Vermeer from the rest of his family, proposing that those many children had been his wife’s “decision” (how this would have been accomplished is not explained). Thus the creator of some of the world’s most transcendent visions of women at home is portrayed as a man existentially alienated from the women with whom he lived.

The other big poser is why Collegiants, who rejected even the streamlined, whitewashed spectacle of Calvinist churches, would have chosen to commission exquisitely crafted, luminously beautiful oil paintings for veneration—a practice smacking loudly of the Romish customs that had occasioned those imaginary gritted teeth. At one point Graham-Dixon proposes that three Vermeer paintings described in 1683 as being in “boxes” were meant to be opened and closed in the manner of Catholic altarpieces.

What is perplexing is that these overreaches seem so unnecessary. Given Collegiant tolerance, Vermeer could have been a Collegiant and a Catholic and a contented paterfamilias. The problem isn’t with Graham-Dixon’s theory. It’s with the assertion of certainty—the reduction of complexity to something that opens with a single key. This is the great paradox of Vermeer’s afterlife: so many smart, capable, inquisitive writers, smitten with the pictures’ elusiveness, working so hard to wrestle that elusiveness into submission.

“Many people,” Graham-Dixon writes of the paintings, “have fallen under their spell, and have wondered what secrets they might hold.” But what if there are no secrets? No riddle to solve, no hidden meanings, covert technologies, arcane symbolism, familial psychodrama, concealed religious convictions? Now that we can see beneath the surfaces of the paintings, we know how carefully Vermeer nudged them toward visual clarity and narrative ambiguity. He painted out the man and dog that once stood behind the sleeping maid, obliterating the easy story line. Woman with a Balance was long read as warning against vanity until imaging proved the pans of her scale to be empty. What keeps us stuck in front of Vermeer paintings for so long is as much about what is withheld as it is about what is shown. Vermeer doesn’t tell us what to think, or even really what was going on—again and again he arranges things so you cannot know.

Perhaps this ambiguity is not a problem to be remedied but a quality to be celebrated, an invitation to take the world as it comes, to recognize how, with small bits of tweaking, we can learn to see the small and local as one with something larger. Graham-Dixon himself writes beautifully about the essential absence of Vermeer: “He is like the visitor in the painting of the woman sleeping, who has just pushed back his chair and gone somewhere else…. However close we come to him, he has always left the room by the time we get there.” His absence isn’t a void awaiting meaning but a form of meaning in itself.

In Caledonian Road, O’Hagan tells us that the fictional Vermeer biography “appeared to its many readers to argue that unknowability is an essential feature of the artistic life, and perhaps of all lives.” But O’Hagan chooses not to tell us whether this is what its author intended.

entries.title: Yemen: The Endless Siege
entries.summary: The “Yemen Model” of American foreign policy has proved a catastrophic failure, leaving brutal proxies better armed and ordinary Yemenis less safe.
entries.source: The New York Review of Books
entries.content:
A swath of green runs through the city of Taiz, in Yemen’s southwestern highlands. From one of the craggy hills surrounding it, the strip resembles an urban planner’s modest attempt at a park. Close-up you can see that the beige of concrete blocks is split by tangles of trees and bushes sprouting from shell-pocked streets: this is no-man’s-land, nature reclaiming a place that has become too deadly for human life.

“The destroyed building there—that’s the beginning of the front line,” Abdulmalek al-Rabadi, a United Nations official who has worked to get humanitarian aid into the city, told me when I last visited a few years ago. We were looking down from an apartment block whose sides had been blown out by rocket fire, at territory controlled by the rebel group known as the Houthis. We had been told not to point, lest our gestures attract a sniper’s bullets. “Nobody is living there,” he said.

Taiz is spread over a basin encircled by hills that each side in Yemen’s decade-old civil war has fought for, lost, recaptured, and lost again. The city has been divided since April 2015, split by a front line that separates the Houthi rebels in the north from a rabble of militias, brigades, and armed groups in the south; most of the competing parties have, at one stage or another, tried to choke the routes bringing supplies into Taiz. The siege is now the lengthiest in modern history: more than twenty times longer than Stalingrad’s, three times longer than Sarajevo’s, longer than even the siege of Troy by more than a year.

Since 2014, after the Houthis seized power and Saudi Arabia responded with air strikes, Yemen has been pounded into near oblivion by warring factions. Iran has strengthened its support for the Houthis, while Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates have armed and enabled a crew of militias that occasionally masquerade as an “internationally recognized government” and just as frequently fight one another for territory. Figures are hard to come by, but in 2018 Save the Children estimated that some 85,000 children under five had starved to death in the conflict, and in 2021 the UN projected that around 154,000 people would have been killed in the fighting and some 223,000 would have died from famine and preventable diseases such as cholera and diphtheria if the war continued through the end of that year. It has gone on for almost five more years. The real toll of this war is likely much higher, but there are no updated and authoritative nationwide assessments because the systems for counting deaths no longer exist.

Though Saudi Arabia and the UAE are nominally allies, their interests in Yemen are at cross-purposes, and since the beginning of the war they have supported different proxies with different aims. (It is unacceptable to the Saudis, for instance, that Emirati-backed groups have joined in southern Yemen’s efforts to secede from the north, while the Emiratis have often been irked by Saudi backing for groups that are seen to be close to the Muslim Brotherhood and other political Islamists.) Last winter the UAE-supported Southern Transitional Council (STC), a coalition of political groups and militias, seized power in the south. Saudi-backed militias—including a new one called Nation Shield, which was formed specifically to oppose the STC—then counterattacked, taking over border security in vital sea- and airports. In late December Saudi forces bombed an Emirati shipment of arms they alleged was headed to the STC. The Emiratis then withdrew from the country, and the STC, one of the most effective anti-Houthi forces, was sidelined.

The Houthis watched the fallout from the mountainous north and plotted their next move. Since the first months of Israel’s assault on Gaza in response to Hamas’s attacks on October 7, 2023, the group has periodically launched long-range missiles and drones at Israel. It has also held Red Sea shipping for ransom in the name of the Palestinian cause, provoking bombardments by the US, the United Kingdom, and Israel. When the US and Israel went to war in Iran earlier this year, the Houthis struck a deal not to attack US ships on the Red Sea. (They did, however, bomb Israel in support of their allies in Iran.)

Yemen is both blessed and cursed by geography. The Bab al-Mandeb Strait, which separates Yemen from East Africa, is a crucial choke point for global shipping, lying on the other side of the Arabian Peninsula from the Strait of Hormuz. In 2015 the Houthis managed to control the strait for a while until an Emirati-backed offensive pushed them back up the coast and established a fiefdom there for Tareq Saleh, a nephew of Yemen’s late authoritarian dictator Ali Abdullah Saleh. His control lasted until this September, when the Houthis surged out of their mountain strongholds and launched a lightning advance down the western coast. By September 11 they had seized the city of Mokha and effectively taken control of the Yemeni flank of the strait, a huge stretch of territory from which the group now has the ability to target international shipping. As of this writing Saudi and Yemeni forces claim to have retaken several crucial areas around the strait; the Houthis deny losing the territory. By late September, meanwhile, the Houthis had resumed their assault on Taiz with waves of attacks. The renewed fighting has killed hundreds and accelerated a spiral of misery that, for Yemen’s civilians, seems to have no end in sight.

Until the recent Houthi offensive, the contours of Yemen’s conflict had remained frozen for about a decade. The underlying divisions, for that matter, existed well before the current war. In 1918 the Mutawakkilite Kingdom of Yemen, in the north of the country, became independent amid the collapse of the Ottoman Empire, and it was ruled by an imam from Sanaa, the capital. The south was controlled by the British from their colony in Aden, a major port since the opening of the Suez Canal in 1869, via a patchwork of London-aligned emirates.

The 1960s was a time of conflict in both the north and the south. In 1962 a coup unseated the imam in Sanaa, and a brutal civil war pitted Egyptian-backed republican forces against Saudi- and British-backed insurgents who supported the deposed monarch.1 So effective were the imam’s guerrillas (many of whom were drawn from the same Zaydi tribal communities of the northern highlands that today form the Houthis’ base) that Gamal Abdel Nasser, Egypt’s fiercely anticolonialist president, lamented to the US ambassador that Yemen had become his “Vietnam.”

As the war in the north wound down, the southern Yemenis won their independence from Great Britain and created the socialist state of South Yemen, which existed from 1967 until 1990, when Yemen was unified under Ali Abdullah Saleh. If you look at a map today, the Houthi-controlled areas broadly match the old boundaries of North Yemen.

In the years since, the US has taken over from Great Britain as Yemen’s Western meddler-in-chief. The Yemen Model, by the RAND Corporation political scientist Alexandra Stark, gives an unusually clear-eyed appraisal of how decades of US policy created the conditions for a war that destroyed the state it was supposed to strengthen. The book scrutinizes the strategy of the George W. Bush administration, which propped up Saleh’s dictatorship. In exchange Saleh gave wide latitude to US special forces as they launched missions to eliminate members of al-Qaeda, which had taken root in Yemen in the 1990s.

Funding for this campaign came from a new piece of legislation enacted in 2005 as part of a National Defense Authorization Act, which allowed the Defense Department broad leeway to bankroll “train-and-equip” missions for counterterrorism without much congressional oversight. Over the next decade some $400 million would be spent this way in Yemen. But what looked like a low-touch way to deal with terrorism in reality funneled dollars to unreliable partners.

In the mid-2000s a militia connected to the northern al-Houthi family—inspired by a religious revival movement and enraged by what its members saw as encroachment on their traditional land by Sunni Yemenis returning to the country after migrating to other parts of the Middle East—decided to take up arms against Saleh. The group was made up of Zaydi Shia Muslims,2 and it drew inspiration from Iran’s Shia revolutionaries. (Saleh himself was also a Zaydi but not strictly sectarian: some powerful figures in his government were Sunni.) For Saleh this group—which called itself Ansar Allah, the Partisans of God, but soon became known as the Houthis—was the perfect boogeyman, and he requested yet more resources to fight it. Proponents of this counterterrorism strategy, Stark writes, ignored the “moral hazard” it created: Saleh’s government was incentivized not to end terrorism but to perpetuate it in order to continue receiving American aid.

After Barack Obama, who had promised to reduce American involvement in the Middle East, took office, his national security team lauded what had become known in Washington circles as the “Yemen model”—a “lighter-footprint approach,” Stark writes, of launching drone strikes against terror groups using what one official called “intelligence-driven, dynamic targeting.” To do so, the US was willing to work with the brutal and corrupt Yemeni army and even, as a former intelligence translator once told me in Aden, with Russian troops. It also grossly understated the number of civilians its strikes killed, including by counting “all military-age males in a strike zone as combatants,” according to The New York Times.3 As Stark points out, each civilian death had the effect of radicalizing Yemenis against both the US and their own government. In 2009 al-Qaeda’s Yemeni and Saudi factions merged to form a more potent and dangerous group.
